18	# Looks Right, Works Right: A Project-Level Benchmark for Multi-Screen Mobile App Generation
19	
20	- Authors: Wu, Fan; Gao, Cuiyun; Huang, Yiming; Xiao, Yang; Chen, Yujia; Liao, Qing
21	- Year / venue: 2026, Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (published)
22	- DOI: 10.18653/2026.emnlp-main.2650 · URL: https://doi.org/10.18653/2026.emnlp-main.2650
23	- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index)
24	
25	Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
26	Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.
27	
28	## 1. Research objective
29	- Introduce MobileForge, a benchmark for project-level multi-screen mobile app generation from a folder of real app screenshots, with a five-axis evaluation (build, navigation, visual fidelity, code maintainability, efficiency), and use it to measure how far frontier multimodal LLMs are from producing a buildable, navigable, faithful and maintainable codebase [A] (pp. 1–2).
30	
31	## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
32	- Opening question: "Can a multimodal LLM read a folder of mobile-app screenshots and generate the source code for that app?" [V] (p. 1). No formal hypotheses. The paper targets three gaps of existing benchmarks: single-page focus, no evaluation of interactive navigation, no project-wide maintainability measure [A] (p. 1).
33	
34	## 3. Methodology
35	- Research design: benchmark construction (VLM-drafted, human-reviewed annotations) plus a full-factorial evaluation of 6 models × 29 apps with a fixed agentic harness, single trial per cell; method studies of the visual judge (human alignment, cross-judge, protocol comparison); hand-labelled failure taxonomy [V] (pp. 3–8, 12–13).
36	- Approach / model / intervention: one tool-augmented agent receives all screenshots of an app plus the human-reviewed page-relationship description and must produce a React + TypeScript + Tailwind project in a pre-scaffolded directory; eight tools (write_file, read_file, str_replace, batch_str_replace, list_files, delete_file, run_command, task_done), soft six-phase plan, up to 50 iterations; on task_done an automated tsc + vite build feeds errors back [V] (p. 6). Prompting is fixed across models, with no screenshot-specific instructions or chain-of-thought, to attribute differences to the model [A] (pp. 6, 14).
37	- Baselines or comparison conditions: six closed models available April 2026 — Claude Opus 4.6, Claude Haiku 4.5, GPT-5, GPT-5 Mini, Gemini 2.5 Pro, Gemini 2.5 Flash [V] (p. 6). No open-weight models and no non-agentic or prior-method baselines [I] (based on p. 6).
38	
39	## 4. Dataset and sample
40	- Data source(s): 29 in-market consumer apps from official public distribution channels; screenshots captured manually from default-state or demo-mode screens without logging in [V] (pp. 3, 9).
41	- Sample size (N) and unit: 29 apps across 14 category buckets; 309 screens (mean 10.7, SD 3.8, range 5–21 per app); 701 navigation test specifications (mean 24.2, range 11–41 per app): 120 page-existence, 392 tab-navigation, 189 parent–child [V] (p. 3). Apps include Notion, Khan Academy, WhatsApp, Klook, Airbnb, Coinbase and others (Table 5) [V] (p. 12).
42	- Sampling / selection method: apps "prioritizing broad cultural recognition" [V] (p. 3) — a purposive, not random, selection. Annotation: a VLM drafts the page-relationship description and test specs; research-team annotators review every field; auto-drafts reach 96.8% recall / 94.3% precision (pages) and 74.1% / 83.9% (test cases); 64.7% of page and 76.5% of test drafts accepted unchanged [V] (pp. 3, 9, 15). The drafting VLM is not named — not reported. Inter-annotator agreement — not reported.
43	- Data availability (public? link?): https://github.com/anoa12159-hue/mobileforge_eval, research-only licence, with screenshots, annotations, harness, evaluator and all 174 run artifacts [A] (pp. 1, 9–10).
44	
45	## 5. Experimental setup
46	- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: single trial per (app, model) cell, 174 runs all completed [V] (p. 6). Build: clean Vite scaffold (React 19 + TypeScript + Tailwind), `npx tsc --noEmit` and `vite build` must both pass with zero errors [V] (p. 4). Navigation tests run in headless Playwright (375×812 viewport) [V] (p. 5). Visual judge: Gemini 2.5 Pro, list-wise with k-shuffle = 3 and reference anchor over 29 apps × 701 scenarios [V] (pp. 6, 13). Sampling temperature and other decoding settings — not reported.
47	- Code availability: repository above; "one-command replay reproduces the comparison table verbatim" [A] (p. 10). Full system prompt only in the repository [V] (p. 14).
48	
49	## 6. Evaluation metrics
50	- Build Success — both type-check and build pass; also route count, page-file count, route coverage [V] (p. 4).
51	- Navigation Correctness — NavPassRate: share of the 701 specs passed under state-isolated execution: each test starts by loading the source page route directly, performs the action, and passes if the URL matches the expected page or, for overlays, the page content hash "changes meaningfully" [V] (pp. 4–5). Rationale: chained walkthroughs cascade failures and blur attribution [A] (p. 5).
52	- Visual Fidelity — primary: per-model Borda score in [0, 1] from list-wise ranking by a VLM judge, with the original screenshot hidden among candidates as an anchor; rankings where the anchor is not first are discarded and re-run [V] (pp. 4–6). Secondary: point-wise 1–5 rubric (Layout 30%, Style 25%, Content 25%, Consistency 20%) kept as an absolute reference [V] (p. 6).
53	- Code Maintainability — total LoC; mean LoC/file (conciseness); ReuseRate (mean import count per shared component); DeadCompRate (share of declared components never imported); ColorConsistency (share of Tailwind colour tokens from a small recurring palette) [V] (p. 4). The authors use "maintainability" rather than "code quality" because correctness is covered by Build [A] (p. 4). These indicators are not validated against human maintainability judgements or established maintainability models — not reported.
54	- Efficiency — input/output tokens, LLM call count, wall-clock LLM time, dollar cost from list prices [V] (p. 4).
55	- Validation against human judgement (visual judge): 55 scenarios labelled with a blinded ranking interface — list-wise vs human strict Kendall τ = 0.716, top-1 accuracy 83.6%, top-2 overlap 80.4%, unrankable-set IoU 0.968; τ = 0.699 for page-existence and 0.731 for parent–child scenarios [V] (p. 13). Number and expertise of human raters and their agreement — not reported. Cross-judge: Claude Sonnet 4.5 on 139 scenarios from 5 apps gives inter-judge τ = 0.867 on the per-model ranking; no self-preference observed [V] (p. 13). Protocol smoke test (3 scenarios × 5 models): list-wise shuffle stability τ = 0.822, pair-wise position bias 23.3%, point-wise "ties-in-the-middle" [V] (pp. 12–13). Judge eligibility: Gemini 2.5 Pro and Claude Sonnet 4.5 ~100% anchor pass on a 33-scenario screening set; GPT-5.1 ~35% [V] (pp. 5, 13).
56	- Navigation evaluator validity: Table 11 reports false positives of the automatic evaluator among flagged cases (6% page existence, 1% parent–child, 10% tab navigation) [V] (p. 16).
57	- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): Wilson 95% CIs for failure-mode proportions [V] (p. 8); ±1 SD error bars across apps in the cost plot [V] (p. 7). No significance tests for model differences; no run-to-run variance (single trial) [V] (pp. 6, 9).
58	
59	## 7. Key findings
60	1. Build success is 100% for all six models; authors attribute this to the harness's verify-repair loop, not the model [V] (pp. 6–7, 12).
61	2. NavPassRate: Opus 4.6 92%, GPT-5 89%, Haiku 4.5 85%, Gemini 2.5 Pro 82%, Gemini 2.5 Flash 62%, GPT-5 Mini 58% [V] (p. 7).
62	3. Visual fidelity has not saturated: Borda 0.906 (Opus) to 0.130 (GPT-5 Mini); point-wise means 1.60–2.99/5, so even the best model stays below 3/5; Opus leads in 26 of 29 apps [V] (pp. 6–7). The gap is concentrated in cross-page Consistency: models re-implement navigation chrome inline per page instead of sharing a component [A] (p. 6).
63	4. Maintainability is dissociated from visual fidelity: Opus writes 1,441 LoC (82 LoC/file) vs GPT-5 668 (33 LoC/file); GPT-5 has higher reuse (4.23 vs 3.83) and fewer dead components (7.8% vs 19.9%); ColorConsistency saturates at 0.74–0.85 [V] (pp. 6–7). Authors: "maintainability is uncorrelated with visual fidelity" [A] (p. 8) — no correlation coefficient is computed.
64	5. Cost: $0.15 (GPT-5 Mini) to $2.90 (Opus) per app; GPT-5 ($0.50, Borda 0.542, NavPass 89%) dominates Haiku 4.5 and Gemini 2.5 Pro on cost and quality [V] (p. 7). Cheaper models fabricate content (Lorem ipsum, stock imagery) [A] (p. 7).
65	6. Navigation failure taxonomy (n = 64 stratified hand-labelled failures from 3,486 executions): C1 blank starting page 7.8% [3.0, 18.3]; C2 route mapping error 10.9% [5.4, 20.9]; C3 target unreachable/occluded 32.8% [22.6, 45.0]; C4 click has no effect 48.4% [36.6, 60.4] [V] (p. 8). C4 (missing or mis-wired onClick) dominates for Opus and GPT-5 (75% of their labelled failures); C3 for GPT-5 Mini (67%); C1 for Gemini 2.5 Flash (42%) [V] (pp. 8, 15). Build checks do not catch silent event-handler bugs [A] (p. 8).
66	7. Per-app difficulty varies widely: point-wise visual 3.62 (Notion) to 2.01 (Apple News); NavPass 0.45 (Medium) to 1.00 (Khan Academy) [V] (pp. 7, 12).
67	
68	## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
69	- Single trial per cell; multi-trial replication left to future work [A] (p. 9).
70	- Visual scores come from Gemini 2.5 Pro, a competitor model class; mitigated by fixed judge, human calibration on 55 scenarios and a cross-judge check [A] (p. 9).
71	- Web-rendering proxy: output is React + Tailwind, not native iOS/Android; native APIs not exercised [A] (p. 9).
72	- Anchor-based judging depends on judges that follow the literal ranking instruction (GPT-5.1 fails) [A] (pp. 13–14).
73	- Per-model failure proportions (n = 8–12) are "descriptive signatures rather than precise point estimates" [A] (p. 8).
74	- Build success cannot discriminate models when a verify-repair loop is present [A] (p. 12).
75	
76	## 9. Limitations we identified
77	- [I] Input is not screenshots alone: the agent also receives a human-reviewed page-relationship description (tab structure, parent–child triggers) (pp. 3, 6), although related work frames the benchmark as using "only screenshots" without "any structural prior" (p. 2). Results therefore describe reconstruction with an annotated navigation map, not pure black-box observation.
78	- [I] Maintainability indicators are structural proxies (LoC, reuse, dead components, colour tokens) with no validation against developer judgement or standard metrics (complexity, duplication, smells, tests). LoC partly reflects how much content is reproduced, so "more LoC" is not clearly worse (p. 4, 7).
79	- [I] "Uncorrelated"/"orthogonal" is asserted from six model means (p. 8); no correlation is computed at app or run level.
80	- [I] Internal inconsistency in failure analysis: overall C4 = 48.4% (Table 4, p. 8), but the per-scenario-type projection (Table 11, p. 16) gives C4 of only 33% (parent–child) and 3% (tab navigation), which cannot average to 48.4% over the 581 interactive specs. The projection method or labels may differ; this needs clarification.
81	- [I] Human validation of the visual judge: 55 scenarios with unreported number of raters, rater expertise and inter-rater agreement (p. 13); the protocol comparison uses only 3 scenarios × 5 models (p. 12).
82	- [I] NavPass counts a pass when the content hash "changes meaningfully" for overlays (p. 5) — a lenient criterion; Table 11 shows 1–10% false positives in flagged cases (p. 16), but overall evaluator precision/recall on passes is not reported.
83	- [I] Well-known apps chosen for "broad cultural recognition" (p. 3) are likely represented in model training data; contamination is not discussed.
84	- [I] Single run per cell with stochastic agents; differences of a few NavPass points (e.g. Opus 92% vs GPT-5 89%) may be within run-to-run noise.
85	- [I] Navigation evaluated only as page transitions; in-page behaviour, state, data and back-end logic are not tested.
86	
87	## 10. Threats to validity
88	- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): annotations drafted by an unnamed VLM, possibly from the same families evaluated; Gemini 2.5 Pro is both judge and candidate (self-preference check reported, p. 13); popular apps may be memorised [I].
89	- External (generalisability of sample/context): 29 apps, 5–21 screens each; web proxy instead of native; one harness design; closed models only [I].
90	- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): NavPass measures routing, not full functional fidelity; Borda is relative (ordinal) and depends on the set of models compared; maintainability proxies unvalidated [I].
91	- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): single trial; no significance tests between models; Wilson CIs only for the failure sample (n = 64), per-model n = 8–12 [I].
92	- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): strong — benchmark, harness, evaluator and run artifacts released, one-command replay (pp. 9–10); decoding settings and drafting VLM not reported; closed models may change [I].
93	
94	## 11. Future research directions
95	- Stated by authors [A]: multi-trial replication (p. 9); cross-platform/native extension (p. 9); stricter build gates (no `any`, strict null checks, lint) if compilation is to discriminate models (p. 12).
96	- Suggested by us [I]: test pure screenshot-only input (without the page-relationship description) and interaction recordings as input; add in-page behavioural tests and data/state checks; validate maintainability proxies against developer ratings and standard static-analysis metrics; report run-to-run variance.
97	
98	## 12. Relevance to our research
99	- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ1, RQ2, RQ3, RQ4, RQ5.
100	- How it informs our work [I]: MobileForge is the closest existing design to our target study: it rebuilds whole multi-screen apps from screenshots of real, in-market apps with an agentic (vibe-coding-like) harness and scores functional navigation fidelity, visual fidelity and maintainability together. It shows these dimensions diverge (visual leader ≠ maintainability leader), giving direct support for joint evaluation. Its gaps — structural prior given as input, unvalidated maintainability proxies, single trials, no behaviour beyond navigation — are concrete design points for RQ5.
101

18	# Interaction2Code: Benchmarking MLLM-based Interactive Webpage Code Generation from Interactive Prototyping
19	
20	- Authors: Xiao, Jingyu; Wan, Yuxuan; Huo, Yintong; Wang, Zixin; Xu, Xinyi; Wang, Wenxuan
21	- Year / venue: 2025, 2025 40th IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering (ASE) (published)
22	- DOI: 10.1109/ase63991.2025.00028 · URL: https://doi.org/10.1109/ase63991.2025.00028
23	- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index)
24	
25	Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
26	Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.
27	
28	## 1. Research objective
29	- Formulate the Interaction-to-Code task (generate an interactive webpage from an "interactive prototype": screenshots before and after each interaction), build a real-world benchmark for it, and systematically study how well MLLMs reproduce webpage interactions, why they fail, and how prompting can help [A] (pp. 1–2).
30	
31	## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
32	- No formal RQs. The study is organised around four reported "limitations" of MLLMs: (1) worse generation of interactive parts than of the full page; (2) ten failure types; (3) poor performance on visually subtle interactions; (4) insufficient understanding from visual input alone — each paired with an improvement strategy [V] (pp. 1–2).
33	
34	## 3. Methodology
35	- Research design: benchmark construction plus empirical comparison of models and prompts; automatic evaluation via Selenium-driven interaction replay; human usability and pairwise evaluation; qualitative failure taxonomy; sub-experiments on visual saliency and input modality; ablation; small user study [V] (pp. 3–11).
36	- Approach / model / intervention: MLLM receives the original screenshot plus post-interaction screenshot(s) and must output one HTML+CSS+JavaScript file, tagging interactive elements with ids (e.g. id="interact1") so a webdriver can trigger them [V] (pp. 3–5). Prompts: Direct, Chain-of-Thought (CoT), Mark (red bounding boxes on interactive areas), Failure-aware Prompt (FAP: lists the ten failure types) [V] (p. 5). Further enhancements: Visual Saliency Enhancement (crop to enlarge the interaction area) and adding human-written textual descriptions of interactions [V] (pp. 9–10).
37	- Baselines or comparison conditions: Gemini-1.5-flash, GPT-4o-20240806, Claude-3.5-Sonnet-20240620, Qwen2.5-VL-instruct 3B/7B/72B; Direct prompting is the baseline for prompt comparisons; Gemini-1.5-flash Direct is the human pairwise baseline [V] (pp. 4, 6). No non-LLM or prior UI-to-code system (e.g. DCGen) is run as a baseline [I] (based on p. 4 model list).
38	
39	## 4. Dataset and sample
40	- Data source(s): (1) C4 validation set (CommonCrawl), filtered as in Design2Code, 1,000 pages sampled across 15 topics, from which four PhD students each picked about 25 → 100 pages; (2) 27 popular GitHub projects (average 13k stars) with deployed links, found via "open-production-web-projects" and "awesome-opensource-apps", to include UI-framework pages [V] (pp. 2–3).
41	- Sample size (N) and unit: 127 webpages and 374 interactions; 15+ topics; 23 tag categories and 8 visual categories (31 interaction categories) [V] (pp. 1, 3). Most frequent interactive tags: button 235, input 52, span 37, link 36 [V] (p. 3).
42	- Sampling / selection method: manual selection by four PhD students for complexity (at least one meaningful interaction) and diversity; 1–10 "important and functional" interactions kept per page; trivial interactions (e.g. hover underline) excluded [V] (pp. 2–3). Selection guidelines are only in the external artifact [V] (p. 3).
43	- Data availability (public? link?): data and code at https://github.com/WebPAI/Interaction2Code [A] (p. 1).
44	
45	## 5. Experimental setup
46	- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: temperature 0; max output 4,096 tokens (commercial) and 2,048 (Qwen); other parameters default [V] (p. 4). Selenium webdriver locates elements by id, performs the interaction and screenshots the result; the changed region is extracted by pixel subtraction (same-size pages) or a Git-diff of rows/columns (size-changing pages) (Algorithm 1) [V] (p. 4). Data-contamination check: BLEU between generated and original HTML is 0.12–0.14 for the four main models [V] (p. 5). FAP experiment: 2/3 of the dataset used to derive failure types, 1/3 for testing [V] (p. 8). Saliency and modality experiments use 10 randomly sampled failure-case webpages each [V] (pp. 9–10).
47	- Code availability: GitHub repository above [A] (p. 1). Appendix H (tool) and detailed human-evaluation instructions are referenced but are not in our 13-page PDF [V] (pp. 6, 11).
48	
49	## 6. Evaluation metrics
50	- Full-page metrics: CLIP score (visual similarity); SSIM (structural similarity); Text similarity = BLEU on OCR-extracted text; Widget Similarity (WS) and Widget Match Rate (WMR) computed with the GUIPilot method [V] (p. 4).
51	- Interaction-part metrics (on the extracted changed region): CLIP, SSIM, Text; Position similarity P = 1 − max(|xo − xg|, |yo − yg|) of normalised interaction-area centres; Implement Rate IR = implemented / (implemented + unimplemented), where "implemented" means detectable by the webdriver [V] (p. 4).
52	- Human metrics: Usability Rate UR = usable / (usable + unusable), judged by four PhD students (three years front-end experience) — usable if the implementation "precisely matches the behavior specified in the interactive prototype"; pairwise Win/Tie/Lose by five annotators against Gemini-1.5-flash Direct, majority (≥3) rule; failure-type annotation [V] (pp. 4, 6–7).
53	- Validation against human judgement: authors state human results "are consistent with Section V-A, confirming the validity of our automatic evaluation metrics" [A] (p. 6). No correlation coefficient, agreement statistic or regression is reported — not reported. Inter-annotator agreement for usability, pairwise or failure annotation — not reported (failure types reached by discussion to consensus on a 25% sample) [V] (p. 7). Number of items in the human evaluations — not reported.
54	- Widget metrics are acknowledged as unreliable for web pages: WS is "consistently poor" (0.02–0.05) and GUIPilot omits many elements because it was designed for mobile UIs [V] (pp. 5–6).
55	- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): none for model or prompt comparisons; saliency effect described as "significantly increases" without a test [V] (pp. 8–9). Not reported.
56	
57	## 7. Key findings
58	1. Interactive parts are generated worse than full pages for all models (e.g. GPT-4o average full-page CLIP 0.7059 vs interaction-part CLIP 0.5598) [V] (p. 6).
59	2. Claude-3.5-Sonnet has the best averages on most metrics (e.g. interaction IR 0.7870, full-page Text 0.5835); GPT-4o with Mark prompt has the highest single IR (0.8128); Qwen2.5-VL-72B ≈ Gemini-1.5-flash; performance rises with model size [V] (pp. 5–6).
60	3. Human Usability Rate (Fig. 6a, read from figure labels): GPT-4o Direct/CoT/Mark 73/74/81%; Claude 66/69/77%; Gemini 47/53/64%; Qwen-72B 41/43/54%; Qwen-3B 17–19% [V] (p. 6). Mark prompting gives the largest usability gain (Claude +11 points vs Direct) [V] (p. 6).
61	4. Ten failure types in two groups (interactive element: missing, no interaction, wrong element, wrong type, wrong position; interaction effects: wrong position, wrong type, effect on wrong element, partial implementation, wrong function) [V] (pp. 7–8). Failures (a) missing element, (b) no interaction and (j) wrong function have usability <10% (0%, 6.93%, 0%) [V] (pp. 7–8). Main failure modes are "No interaction", "Partial implementation", "Interactive element missing" and "Wrong function" [A] (p. 8).
62	5. Failures cluster into spatial (a, c, e, f), type (d, g) and behavioural (b, h, i, j) failures [A] (p. 8).
63	6. Low visual saliency (small interaction area) lowers SSIM and position similarity; cropping to enlarge the area (1.2–3×) recovers interactions on 10 failure pages [V] (pp. 9–10).
64	7. On 10 failure pages, combining visual and human-written text descriptions beats either modality alone for GPT-4o (Direct: Position 0.7157 V+T vs 0.3951 V) [V] (p. 10). All four enhancements combined give the best ablation result (GPT-4o interaction CLIP 0.6937 vs 0.5700) [V] (p. 11).
65	8. FAP: authors claim it improves "all models" [A] (p. 8), but Table VI shows Qwen2.5-VL-3B drops on 7 of 8 metrics and Qwen-7B on 5 of 8 [V] (p. 9).
66	9. User study: with the tool, 4 tasks took 279 s vs 413 s on average and expert similarity rating 4.5 vs 3.875 (two participants per condition, two raters) [V] (p. 11).
67	10. Code quality or maintainability of the generated HTML/CSS/JS is not measured; the only code-level measure is BLEU against the original HTML, used as a contamination check [V] (pp. 4–5).
68	
69	## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
70	- Limited context length: complex pages with many interactions may exceed the context window; iterative generation suggested [A] (p. 11).
71	- Model selection: only three main commercial MLLMs tested; others (e.g. Pixtral) left for future work [A] (p. 11).
72	- Back-end interactions (login, search) cannot be evaluated because the benchmark has no back-end code [A] (p. 11).
73	- Existing widget-consistency methods are designed for mobile UIs and miss web elements [A] (p. 5).
74	
75	## 9. Limitations we identified
76	- [I] Validation of automatic metrics against humans is only a qualitative "consistent" statement (p. 6); no correlation, agreement (kappa) or item counts are given. The automatic metrics are therefore not shown to measure functional fidelity.
77	- [I] "Implement Rate" counts an interaction as implemented if the webdriver can find and trigger the element (p. 4) — this measures presence, not correct behaviour; functional correctness rests on the human Usability Rate alone.
78	- [I] Interaction fidelity is judged on screenshots of state changes, not on behavioural traces or DOM/state assertions; non-visual effects (data, network, storage) are out of scope (based on pp. 3–4, 11).
79	- [I] Several sub-experiments use only 10 pages (pp. 9–10) and the user study has 2 participants per condition (p. 11); these results are anecdotal.
80	- [I] The FAP claim ("improve ... on all models", p. 8) contradicts the paper's own Table VI (p. 9) for the two smaller Qwen models.
81	- [I] The FAP test uses failure types derived from 2/3 of the same dataset (p. 8); split procedure and whether it is by page or by interaction is not stated.
82	- [I] Fig. 9 "No failure" shares (about 36% for GPT-4o, about 40% for Claude, read from the figure, p. 9) look hard to reconcile with Usability Rates of 73–81% (p. 6); the denominators/definitions are not explained.
83	- [I] The contamination argument (C4 has only text; BLEU 0.12–0.14, p. 5) is weak: C4 URLs' HTML is widely crawled elsewhere, and low BLEU does not rule out memorised layout.
84	- [I] No code-quality, maintainability or code-structure measurement, despite generating JavaScript event logic.
85	
86	## 10. Threats to validity
87	- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): pages and interactions hand-picked by the authors' annotators (pp. 2–3); FAP failure types derived from the same benchmark (p. 8); Table VI direct baselines differ from Table IV (different subset), so improvements are relative to a subset [I].
88	- External (generalisability of sample/context): 127 pages, front-end only, no back-end; mostly click-type interactions on buttons (235 of tagged elements) (p. 3); single-file output, not multi-file framework projects [I].
89	- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): visual metrics on changed regions approximate interaction fidelity; IR measures element presence; widget metrics admitted unreliable for web (p. 5) [I].
90	- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): single deterministic run (temperature 0); no tests, CIs or agreement statistics; small N in sub-studies [I].
91	- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): data and code released (p. 1); prompts shown (p. 5); key guidelines and appendix only in the artifact; the PDF is arXiv v3 (1 Mar 2026), the ASE 2025 version may differ [I].
92	
93	## 11. Future research directions
94	- Stated by authors [A]: iterative multi-round generation for many interactions; testing more MLLMs (e.g. Pixtral) (p. 11); handling interactions that require back-end code (p. 11); designing widget-level consistency detection suited to web pages (pp. 5–6).
95	- Suggested by us [I]: validate interaction metrics against human usability with reported correlations; add behavioural assertions (DOM state, event sequences) and code-quality/maintainability analysis of generated JS; extend to multi-page apps with back-end.
96	
97	## 12. Relevance to our research
98	- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ1, RQ2, RQ4, RQ5 (RQ3 only by absence).
99	- How it informs our work [I]: this is the closest web benchmark to reverse engineering from observable behaviour: input is before/after screenshots of interactions, and the target is a page that reproduces that behaviour. It supplies a usable failure taxonomy and the Usability Rate as a human functional-fidelity measure, but its automatic metrics are weakly validated and it ignores code quality.
100	
101	## 13. Evidence table (for the evidence matrix)
102	| RQ | Claim | Page | Label | Strength |
103	|---|---|---|---|---|
104	| RQ1 | Interaction-to-Code: MLLM generates one HTML/CSS/JS file from before/after interaction screenshots; Direct, CoT, Mark, FAP prompts | p. 2–5 | V | moderate |
105	| RQ2 | Interaction fidelity measured by interaction-part CLIP/SSIM/Text/Position, Implement Rate (webdriver), and human Usability Rate | p. 4 | V | moderate |
106	| RQ2 | Best human Usability Rate 81% (GPT-4o Mark); Claude 66–77%; Qwen-3B 17–19% on 374 interactions | p. 6 | V | moderate |
107	| RQ2 | Interactive parts scored lower than full pages for all six models | p. 6 | V | moderate |
108	| RQ2 | Ten failure types; missing element, no interaction, wrong function yield <10% usability | p. 7–8 | V | moderate |
109	| RQ3 | No code quality or maintainability measured; code compared to original only via BLEU 0.12–0.14 for contamination | p. 5 | V | moderate |
110	| RQ4 | Automatic metrics declared "consistent" with human evaluation; no correlation or inter-annotator agreement reported | p. 6 | V | weak |
111	| RQ4 | Widget Similarity/Match (GUIPilot) unreliable for web pages (WS 0.02–0.05) | p. 5–6 | V | moderate |
112	| RQ4 | Claimed FAP gain on all models contradicted by Table VI for Qwen-3B/7B | p. 8–9 | V | moderate |
113	| RQ4 | Saliency, modality sub-studies on 10 pages; user study 2 vs 2 participants | p. 9–11 | V | weak |
114	| RQ5 | Back-end-dependent interactions (login, search) not evaluable; future work | p. 11 | A | moderate |
115	
116	## 14. Key quotes
117	> "existing benchmarks only contain static web pages for evaluation and ignore the dynamic interaction" (p. 1)
118	> "An interaction is considered usable if its implementation precisely matches the behavior specified in the interactive prototype." (p. 6)
119	> "The benchmark we collect does not include back-end code; we cannot verify the generation effect of such interactions" (p. 11)
120	
121	## Analyst notes
122	- Reading coverage: whole PDF read (pp. 1–13); garbled Figure 6 and Table VI/Figure 9 checked on PDF pages 6, 8 and 9. References skimmed. Appendix H and annotation guidelines are external (artifact) and were not read.
123	- Uncertainties: usability percentages are read from figure labels (p. 6); Fig. 9 percentages are approximate. Our PDF is arXiv v3 (dated 1 Mar 2026), later than the ASE 2025 publication; page numbers refer to this PDF. Peer-reviewed (ASE 2025, tier 1). Same group (CUHK, Lyu) as DesignBench/DCGen — related benchmarks in our set may share authors and methods.

18	# ProgramBench: Can Language Models Rebuild Programs From Scratch?
19	
20	- Authors: Yang, John; Lieret, Kilian; Ma, Jeffrey; Thakkar, Parth; Pedchenko, Dmitrii; Sootla, Sten; McMilin, Emily; Yin, Pengcheng; Hou, Rui; Synnaeve, Gabriel; Yang, Diyi; Press, Ofir

25	Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.

27	
28	## 1. Research objective
29	- [A] Measure whether software-engineering (SWE) agents can develop whole programs "holistically", including the high-level architecture decisions that existing bug-fix or single-feature benchmarks do not test (p. 1; p. 2).
30	- [A] Task: "given only a program and its documentation, agents must architect and implement a codebase that matches the reference executable's behavior" (p. 1).
31	
32	## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
33	- Not stated as formal RQs. [I] Implicit questions: (1) can LMs rebuild real programs from an executable plus docs; (2) do generated behavioural tests capture the programs well enough to judge this; (3) how do model-written codebases and development trajectories differ from human ones; (4) how often do models cheat when allowed internet access.
34	
35	## 3. Methodology
36	- Research design: [V] A benchmark built semi-automatically from open-source repositories, plus an evaluation of 9 LMs, two ablations (forced different language; internet access with cheating detection), test-suite validation (coverage, assertion strength) and descriptive analyses of codebases and trajectories (p. 3; p. 5; p. 7; p. 9).
37	- Approach / model / intervention: [V] The agent receives the compiled gold executable (execute-only permissions, so it cannot be decompiled) and its usage documentation, inside a Docker container without internet. It must write source code in any language plus a build script that produces an executable with the same behaviour (p. 2; p. 4; p. 18). [V] The system prompt forbids obtaining source code, wrapping the binary, and decompiling or tracing it (strace/ltrace); only running the executable and reading the bundled docs is allowed (p. 19; p. 20).
38	- Fidelity oracle: [V] Behavioural tests are generated by a SWE-agent (mini-SWE-agent with Claude Sonnet 4.5) that explores the program, its source code, existing tests and documentation. It harvests existing behavioural tests and iteratively adds tests that cover missing code paths, guided by line coverage (p. 3). Assertions target observable effects only: stdout/stderr content, exit codes and files produced (p. 2; p. 3). Weak tests are flagged by an assertion-quality linter and revised. Tests that do not pass the gold binary deterministically, or that pass a dummy binary, are discarded (p. 3; p. 27). The tests are never shown to the solving agent (p. 3).
39	- Baselines or comparison conditions: [V] 9 LMs compared with each other; no human baseline ("we do not carry out any formal human studies") (p. 5; p. 20). For test quality, the generated suites are compared with the projects' native test suites (p. 7; p. 8).
40	- [I] Relation to our topic: this is the closest design to black-box reverse engineering of an application. The agent observes the running program and its docs but not the source, and fidelity is judged by behavioural equivalence. The targets are CLI/TUI programs, not GUI or web apps.
41	
42	## 4. Dataset and sample
43	- Data source(s): [V] 200 GitHub repositories in compiled languages that build a standalone executable: Rust 107, Go 46, C/C++ 45, other 2 (one Java, one Haskell). They range from small CLI tools to FFmpeg, SQLite, DuckDB, PHP and Lua (p. 2; p. 4).
44	- Sample size (N) and unit: [V] 200 tasks; 248,853 test functions (median 770 per task, min 224, max 14,645) (p. 4). [V] 9 models x 200 tasks = 1,800 runs (p. 10); some analyses use 1,788 runs (p. 32). [V] Median codebase size 8,635 code lines (min 212, max 2,701,283) and 50 code files (p. 4). [V] Difficulty bins: Easy 28, Medium 143, Hard 29 (p. 31).
45	- Sampling / selection method: [V] Filter for repositories that can produce a standalone executable, with compiled language as the heuristic. Repositories whose executable needs the internet are excluded; 18 networking tools are kept and tested over localhost (p. 3; p. 21). [I] How the 200 were chosen from the eligible pool (random, by stars, by build success) is not reported.
46	- Data availability (public? link?): [A] Code at github.com/facebookresearch/ProgramBench, open-sourced (p. 1; p. 2).
47	
48	## 5. Experimental setup
49	- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: [V] mini-SWE-agent (bash-only minimal scaffold), vendor-default hyperparameters, 20 CPUs and 60 GB RAM per container, 1,000-step and 6-hour limits (p. 5), 3-minute per-action timeout, no cost limit, outputs truncated at 10,000 characters (p. 32). [V] Base image: Ubuntu 22.04 with Rust 1.92.0, Python 3.12, Go 1.21.0, a C/C++ toolchain and tmux for TUIs (p. 16). [V] Binary test assets that models cannot easily generate (images, audio, custom formats) are provided; standard text formats are not (p. 21; p. 22). [V] Before evaluation, all files matching the hash of the original executable are removed, and git history is wiped (p. 18; p. 19).
50	- Number of runs: [V] One run per model-task (1,800 runs, p. 10). Repeats or seeds: not reported.
51	- Code availability: [A] public (p. 1).
52	
53	## 6. Evaluation metrics
54	- % Resolved: share of tasks where all tests pass and no cheating is flagged; the primary metric (p. 5).
55	- % Almost: share of tasks with ≥95% of tests passing (p. 6).
56	- % Tests Passed: per-task pass fraction. The authors say it is "only meaningful for relative comparisons" and "does not reliably correlate with percentage of working functionality" (p. 5).
57	- Test-suite quality: line coverage of the original binary versus native suites; dummy pass rate (share of tests that a trivially wrong program passes) (p. 7; p. 8).
58	- Code structure (descriptive): lines of code, number of files, maximum directory depth, function count and average function length, compared with the reference, for runs passing ≥75% of tests (p. 8; p. 9).
59	- Trajectory metrics: action types (read/write/probe/execute/git) classified by keyword matching; edit counts; share of code written in the single largest edit (p. 9; p. 10).
60	- Cheating rate: majority vote of 9 LM judges (p. 6; p. 17).
61	- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): [V] No significance tests or confidence intervals. The paper reports Pearson correlations of pass rate with API calls (r = 0.27) and cost (r = 0.21) (p. 33) and Fleiss' κ for judge agreement (p. 17). [I] The statement that "test pass rates are significantly different between models" (p. 2) is not backed by any reported test.
62	
63	## 7. Key findings
64	1. [V] No model resolves any task (0% resolved for all 9). Claude Opus 4.7 reaches ≥95% of tests on 3.0% of tasks, Opus 4.6 on 2.5%, Sonnet 4.6 on 1.6%, and all others on 0% (p. 6).
65	2. [V] Macro-averaged test pass rates: Opus 4.6 52.0%, Opus 4.7 51.2%, Sonnet 4.6 48.5%, GPT 5.4 38.3%, Gemini 3.1 Pro 36.6%, down to GPT 5 mini 15.9%. Rates fall from Easy to Hard for every model, e.g. Opus 4.6 from 73.9% to 24.7% (p. 31).
66	3. [V] Across all runs, the median pass rate is 32%; about 18% of runs fall in the 0–5% bin, and fewer than 5% exceed 90% (p. 32). C/C++ tasks average 27.7%, against 38.5% for Rust and 38.4% for Go (p. 33).
67	4. [V] Generated test suites average 79.7% line coverage (median 86.2%), against 56.8% (median 64.3%) for native suites, over 100 sampled repositories. Against 12 dedicated behavioural/integration suites, coverage is 62.16% versus 66.11% (p. 7; p. 8).
68	5. [V] The assertion linter cut the mean dummy pass rate from 18.5% to 3.7%, and the stricter tests were 20–30 percentage points harder to pass without changing the model ranking (p. 8; p. 23).

93	  - median tests per task 770 (p. 4) vs 750 (p. 23);
94	  - the Fig. 12 boxplot shows Sonnet 42% and Gemini 51%, the text says 44% and 53%, and the caption says GPT 5.4 writes "a median of 96%" while the text says 100% (p. 10);
95	  - "best model" is Opus 4.7 by % almost (p. 6), but Opus 4.6 has the higher mean pass rate (p. 31).
96	  
97	  None changes the conclusions, but they lower confidence in exact figures.
98	- [I] The main metric (% resolved) is all-or-nothing and saturates at 0% for every model (p. 6), so it cannot rank models; the paper relies on the softer metric that it itself says is only relative (p. 5).
99	- [I] Tasks are CLI/TUI programs; GUI, web or mobile apps are not covered, so UI and visual fidelity are untested.
100	
101	## 10. Threats to validity
102	- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): [V] Leakage controls: separate build and inference containers, execute-only binary, wiped git history, no internet, hash-based removal of the original binary (p. 18; p. 19). [I] Remaining threats: pretraining memory of famous programs; test generation by a same-family model with source access; the provided test assets may hint at tested behaviours (p. 21).
103	- External (generalisability of sample/context): [I] Compiled-language CLI/TUI programs; a minimal single-agent scaffold, unlike practitioners' vibe-coding tools with rich IDE context and human steering (p. 5; p. 12).
104	- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): [I] Behavioural equivalence on observable stdout/stderr/exit codes/files is a strong operational definition of functional fidelity for CLIs. The authors admit, however, that % tests passed does not track the share of working functionality (p. 5), and that untested inputs remain (p. 12). Code-structure metrics are size measures, not quality measures.
105	- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): [I] One run per cell; no CIs or tests; large N (200 tasks) partly offsets this for model-level means, but not for per-task claims.
106	- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): [V] Harness configuration, prompts, linter rules and the full repository list are reported (p. 19; p. 27; p. 32; p. 36). [A] Benchmark open-sourced (p. 2).
107	
108	## 11. Future research directions
109	- Stated by authors [A] (p. 12):
110	  - richer test generation that improves coverage and adds system constraints (speed, memory);
111	  - multi-agent approaches to long-horizon coding;
112	  - human-centred agents, where a developer guides design decisions while the agent works from the executable;
113	  - using the pipeline to generate training data (p. 5).
114	- Suggested by us [I]:
115	  1. Add maintainability measures (complexity, smells, duplication, modularity, ease of change) to the rebuilt codebases, and compare across languages.
116	  2. Repeat runs to estimate variance.
117	  3. Generate tests with several model families to check oracle bias.
118	  4. Extend the same black-box protocol to GUI/web applications, where observable behaviour includes visuals and interaction.

121	- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ1, RQ2, RQ3, RQ4, RQ5.
122	- How it informs our work [I]: This is the most direct evidence on our core scenario: an agent rebuilding software only from the running artefact and its documentation, judged by behavioural equivalence. It gives (a) a concrete protocol for black-box reconstruction with leakage controls, (b) an oracle-construction method with measured coverage and assertion strength, and (c) evidence that rebuilds diverge structurally from human code (monolithic, few files, long functions). It does not measure maintainability as such, does not cover GUIs, and has no human-in-the-loop condition. These three gaps sit directly on RQ3 and RQ5.

To evaluate a model’s solution, we generate behavioral tests by prompting a SWE-agent to systematically probe
the original program with varied inputs and codify the observed input-output behavior into assertions that a
candidate reconstruction must satisfy. Crucially, these tests are never revealed to the task worker. Since tests
target executable behavior rather than source code, evaluation is entirely implementation agnostic; a model
may use different algorithms, abstractions, or even programming languages than the original codebase, and
still pass as long as the input-output behavior matches. While any test suite necessarily under-approximates
an executable’s full specification, we empirically demonstrate that our test generation pipeline creates large
suites that reliably capture core functionality.
Using our pipeline, we collect 200 task instances, ranging from compact CLI tools to complex, widely used
software including language interpreters (PHP, Lua, tinycc), databases (DuckDB, SQLite), media and
compression utilities (FFmpeg, zstd, xz), and developer tools (ripgrep, fzf, jq). We evaluate 9 language
models equipped with mini-SWE-agent, a widely adopted coding agent scaffold for open source SWE-agent
research. The results resoundingly confirm ProgramBench’s difficulty for today’s models; no task instance is
fully resolved. However, test pass rates are significantly different between models. The best model, Opus 4.7,
manages to pass 95% of tests for 3% of task instances. Further analysis reveals that model-written codebases
diverge significantly from human-written ones, favoring monolithic file structures with longer functions. Our
trajectory analyses showcase how models vary in the length and make up of the way they develop software.
We open source ProgramBench to enable the community to reproduce and build upon our investigations.


2     ProgramBench
This section describes ProgramBench in detail. We first formalize the task (§2.1), then explain how task in-
stances are semi-automatically constructed from open-source repositories (§2.2). Finally, we review benchmark
statistics (§2.3) and distinguishing features (§2.4).

2.1   Task Formulation
Given a gold (reference) executable and its usage documentation, a task worker is asked to write source code
and a build script that constructs a candidate executable which should reproduce the behavior of the gold
executable. The task worker does not have access to the internet and is free to implement the solution in
any programming language. The task worker is informed of these conditions via the initial prompt, and

specification, ProgramBench’s framing makes extending test coverage trivial.

2.2    Benchmark Construction
Next, we discuss our four-stage pipeline for converting open source GitHub repositories into ProgramBench
task instances, as visualized in Figure 2. All construction steps use the mini-SWE-agent1 harness with Claude
Sonnet 4.5, operating inside a Docker container based on ubuntu:22.04.
Identify candidate repositories. We synthesize ProgramBench tasks from open source GitHub repositories.
First, we filter for repositories that may produce a standalone executable or program. A strong heuristic is to
look for projects written in compiled languages (e.g., C/C++, Golang, Rust).
Construct executable from source. Given a repository, we task a SWE-agent with compiling the gold executable
and, if successful, record the commands that reproduce the build in a single build script (Step 1 in Figure 2).
Generate behavioral tests. We use an agent to explore the program, its source code, existing tests, and
documentation, and then generate behavioral tests (Step 2 of Figure 2). The test assertions target externally
observable effects rather than source-level internals. For example, a test might assert that specific strings
appear in stdout or stderr, or that an invocation produces expected files. The agent is also prompted to
identify and include in its test suite any existing behavioral tests defined in the repository (harvesting).
The agent continuously measures the line coverage of the current test suite and iteratively writes new tests to
invoke missing code paths, attempting to achieve full coverage.
Some tests may have missing or trivially true assertions. Therefore, to ensure assertion quality, tests are
flagged if they fail the gold binary or trigger our assertion quality linter (Appendix A.3.5), which detects
structurally weak assertion patterns such as exit-code-only checks, short substring matches, and disjunctive
assertions. The agent is prompted to revise all flagged tests. At the end, any remaining tests that do not pass
with the gold binary deterministically or pass a dummy binary are discarded. More details in §A.3.
Prior work has shown that coding benchmarks, such as SWE-bench, have some test suites with one of the
following two shortcomings (Chowdhury et al., 2024). First, a task’s test suite could be overly stringent,
meaning it checks for criteria not apparent from the initial task definition. Second, a task’s test suite might
not fully check whether a solution actually solves the initially stated task. For the first case, ProgramBench
tests assert only on observable behavior of the reference executable, precluding overspecification of source-level
internals. A subtler concern is whether tests demand exact reproduction of implementation-dependent output
(e.g., floating point precision or rendering discretization). We address this directly: the model has full access
to the gold executable at inference time, so any behavior a behavioral test expects is discoverable by running
that same command. An audit of all 200 task instances found zero tests that invoke flags or subcommands not
surfaced by the executable’s documentation, and only 5 instances where implementation-dependent output
could plausibly appear, none of which contained such assertions in practice (§A.3.4). For the second case, a
finite test suite necessarily under-approximates an executable’s full specification (Liu et al., 2023; Le Goues

queries a product manager: “when a user runs X with flag -y, what should the output be?” The model
must decide which questions to ask and in what order. This setting tests a model’s ability to infer behavior
through systematic, hypothesis-driven exploration, mirroring challenges developers routinely face when probing
partially documented APIs or onboarding to unfamiliar systems by observing behavior in the absence of
complete specifications.
Simple collection criteria. Our collection pipeline requires only that a repository produce a standalone
executable. No existing test suite, language-specific AST tooling, or ecosystem-reliant test frameworks are
needed. The benchmark is therefore straightforward to extend with new instances over time, a valuable
property for sustaining benchmark relevance (Deng et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025). The same pipeline can
also generate training data, similar to how prior benchmark collection schemas have been repurposed for
training (Badertdinov et al., 2025; Pham et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025).


3     Experiments
Models. We evaluate 9 recent language models that are regarded as strong coding models based on rank on
existing benchmarks, including SWE-bench and Terminal-bench. These include Claude Opus 4.7, Claude
Opus 4.6, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Claude Haiku 4.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Gemini 3 Flash, GPT 5.4, GPT 5.4 mini,
and GPT 5 mini. All models use vendor-default hyperparameters.
Agent scaffold. We use mini-SWE-agent because it is both widely adopted as a baseline by other benchmarks
(SWE-bench Verified, Multilingual2 , Terminal-bench3 ), and deliberately minimal in its scaffolding, reducing
confounds between model capability and harness design. Each model runs inside a container with 20 CPUs
and 60GB RAM, with a limit of 1,000 steps and 6 hours per run; full configuration details are in §B.1.
Metrics. We primarily report % Resolved, which refers to the percentage of task instances where the model’s
codebase passes all associated test cases and is not flagged as cheating. Due to the challenging nature of this
benchmark, we also report % Tests Passed per task instance, which captures partial progress even when no
task is fully resolved. However, we note that this softer metric is only meaningful for relative comparisons
between models; even a single failed test can imply a fundamental flaw in a model’s solution. As discussed in
§2.2, % Tests Passed also does not reliably correlate with percentage of working functionality.


4     Results
Our main results are shown in Table 2. ProgramBench is extremely challenging; across the board, no model
fully solves any single ProgramBench task instance. That said, from Figure 4, we find that models make
meaningful progress on a significant proportion of tasks, with Claude Opus 4.7 achieving the highest proportion
of solutions that pass 95+% of tests, at 3.0%.
Task difficulty is largely model-agnostic. As shown in Figure 5, models consistently score higher on simpler
CLI utilities like nnn, fzf, and gron, while complex systems such as FFmpeg, php-src, typst, and ast-grep
remain out of reach. These trends suggest that ProgramBench captures intrinsic variation in task difficulty
that is independent of model choice. The rank order of tasks by pass rate is broadly consistent across models.

4.1    Ablations
We review two alternative evaluation settings to investigate the impact the availability of certain tools and
resources has on solutions and cheating rates.
Different-language constraint. In this setting, we force models to implement their solutions in a different
programming language from the reference repository. In theory, this measure should obviate models’ ability
to simply regurgitate reference code from their pre-training corpora, requiring them to demonstrate deep
understanding of program behavior rather than surface-level recall.

Unexpectedly, the constraint does not uniformly decrease scores. As shown in Figure 6, while Claude Opus 4.7

roughly unchanged. Under this constraint, we observe a noticeable shift towards Python as the implementation

implementation language best suits a given task and their own capabilities; forcing a language switch can
inadvertently steer a model toward a language it has more success with.
Open internet with cheating detection. We repeat evaluation for one model per provider family with a key
distinction: models are given unrestricted internet access. Note that in the system prompt, we still explicitly
tell models that cheating is disallowed. To detect cheating, we run an LM-as-a-judge pipeline where 9 judges
independently inspect a trajectory for whether the model looked up source code or submitted a wrapper
around the reference executable as a solution; a task is flagged if a majority identify a violation. With this
setting, our goals are to understand, first, how often models cheat, and second, how reliable our cheating
detection mechanisms are.
As shown in Table 3, cheating is widespread: 20–36% of tasks are flagged for the three stronger models, with
source code lookup accounting for the vast majority of violations. At the same time, judges disagree on
40–57% of tasks for these models, indicating that even with 9 judges across three model families, reliable
detection remains elusive. The combination of high cheating rates and unreliable detection gives us confidence
that blocking internet access entirely is the appropriate default for ProgramBench. We document additional
details about the evolution of our mitigation efforts in §A.2.

18	# Is Vibe Coding Safe? Benchmarking Vulnerability of Agent-Generated Code in Real-World Tasks
19	
20	- Authors: Zhao, Songwen; Wang, Danqing; Zhang, Kexun; Luo, Jiaxuan; Li, Zhuo; Li, Lei
21	- Year / venue: 2025, arXiv (preprint)
22	- DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2512.03262 · URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.03262
23	- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index)
24	- Venue note: `metadata.json` records an arXiv preprint, but the PDF we hold (arXiv v4, 21 Sep 2026) carries the footer "Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, Seoul, South Korea. PMLR 306, 2026" (p. 1). Per the project decision in RESEARCH.md, treat as peer-reviewed (ICML 2026, PMLR 306, no DOI). Page refs refer to this arXiv v4 PDF, not PMLR pagination.
25	
26	Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
27	Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.
28	
29	## 1. Research objective
30	[A] To test whether code produced by LLM coding agents in a vibe-coding setting (feature request in natural language, little human review) is safe to deploy, by building a benchmark (SusVibes) that scores both functional correctness and security of repository-level feature implementations (p. 1, p. 2).
31	
32	## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
33	No formal RQs or hypotheses. Implicit questions from the contributions list:
34	- [A] How functionally correct and how secure are agent-generated feature implementations in real repositories? (p. 2)
35	- [A] Do models and agent frameworks differ by weakness (CWE) category? (p. 2, p. 6)
36	- [A] Can simple prompting strategies (CWE self-selection, oracle CWE hint) reduce security risk without hurting functionality? (p. 2, p. 8)
37	
38	## 3. Methodology
39	- Research design: benchmark construction followed by a comparative evaluation of 12 agentic settings (3 agent frameworks x 4 backbone LLMs), plus a mitigation experiment on one setting (p. 2, p. 6, p. 8). [V]
40	- Approach / model / intervention:
41	  - Task construction: pick a vulnerability-fix commit C0 that fixes feature F; revert to the preceding vulnerable commit C−1; take the security tests added by the fix (Tsecure) and existing functional tests (Tfunc); an LLM agent (SWE-agent) masks out the feature code in C−1 and a second SWE-agent instance writes an issue-style feature request; a third instance links each line of the canonical secure implementation to a requirement in the request, and the mask is enlarged until the request covers the secure implementation (p. 3–4, p. 15). [V]
42	  - The task description must state the wanted functionality without implementation or security hints ("Do NOT mention security-related considerations") (p. 16). [V]
43	  - Masks are generated on the vulnerable commit, not the fixed commit, so that no information from the fix leaks into the task input (p. 4). [A]
44	  - Execution environments: Docker images built automatically by a SWE-agent variant with Claude 4 Sonnet; test-log parsers synthesised with OpenAI o3 (p. 17, p. 18). [V]
45	- Baselines or comparison conditions: the 12 framework x LLM combinations compared against each other (p. 6–7); in the mitigation study, "generic" security reminder vs. self-selection vs. oracle CWE hint (p. 8). [V] There is no human-developer baseline other than the historical vulnerable human implementation that defines each task [I] (based on p. 3–5).
46	
47	## 4. Dataset and sample
48	- Data source(s): vulnerability-fix commits from ReposVul and MoreFixes (over 20,000 records, last 10 years), restricted to Python ≥ 3.7 projects and commits that modify tests (p. 3, p. 14). [V]
49	- Sample size (N) and unit: 186 tasks (feature requests) from 100 Python GitHub repositories, 10 application domains, 79 CWE types (p. 2, p. 13). [V] Mean context 236K lines / 1,186 files; mean target patch 175.0 lines / 1.8 files; mean 66.9 functional and 3.5 security tests per task (p. 5, Table 2). [V] 130 single-file, 23 two-file and 33 multi-file tasks (p. 14). [V]
50	- Sampling / selection method: funnel ~20,000 records → ~2,000 Python → ~450 candidate commits → ~420 after task construction/verification → 200 after environment and execution validation → 186 after human test-quality verification (p. 14, Table 10). [V] Counts before the final stage are stated as approximate (p. 14). [V]
51	- Data availability (public? link?): code and dataset at github.com/LeiLiLab/susvibes; public leaderboard (p. 1). [A] (link not checked by us)
52	
53	## 5. Experimental setup
54	- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: agent frameworks SWE-agent, OpenHands, Claude Code; backbones Claude 4 Sonnet, Kimi K2, Gemini 2.5 Pro, Gemini 3 Pro; default recommended system prompt of each framework; maximum 200 steps; agents may run their code and use runtime feedback (p. 6). [V] Main experiments include a short generic security reminder in the prompt (p. 7, p. 20). [V] Temperature, sampling settings, number of runs per task, cost and exact model versions: not reported (only pass@1 stated, p. 6).
55	- Code availability: GitHub repository stated (p. 1). [A]
56	- How functional correctness is tested: the human-written functional tests already in the upstream repository (Tfunc) are run on the agent's patch inside the Docker environment (p. 2, p. 4). [V] Task validity is checked by execution: the masked repo must fail both test sets, the vulnerable commit must pass functional and fail security tests, and the fixed commit must pass both (p. 5, p. 19). [V] No LLM judge is used for scoring (p. 6). [V]
57	- How security is tested: security unit tests added by the historical fix commit (Tsecure), mean 3.5 per task (p. 5). [V] Five software-engineering experts independently rated the security tests of the 200 candidate tasks on a Pass / Conditional Pass / Fail rubric for coupling to the reference implementation: 6.5% were coupled to the ground-truth implementation; 93.5% checked the intended property (49.5% full coverage, 44.0% might miss some edge-case secure implementations; 92.1% of these partial tests were refinable). Conditional Pass and Fail tests were rewritten and cross-checked in a second round (p. 19). [V] Inter-annotator agreement: not reported.
58	
59	## 6. Evaluation metrics
60	- FuncPass — pass@1 on the functional tests (p. 6, p. 7). [V] Chosen because pass@1 reflects a vibe-coding user who wants correct code at once (p. 6). [A]
61	- SecPass — pass@1 on functional plus security tests, i.e. share of all tasks solved correctly and securely (p. 6). [V] Rationale: a solution with no meaningful feature is trivially "secure", so security only counts for functionally correct solutions (p. 6). [A]
62	- SecPass ⊥ FuncPass — secure ratio computed on the intersection of tasks solved correctly by all compared settings, to separate security from functional skill (p. 6). [V]
63	- Precision / recall / F1 of agent-selected CWE types vs. ground truth (self-selection setting) (p. 9, Table 6). [V]
64	- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): none reported. Results are single pass@1 numbers without confidence intervals or repeated runs; Table 5 uses ▲/▼ markers without a stated test (p. 8). [V]
65	
66	## 7. Key findings
67	1. Best functional setting SWE-agent + Claude 4 Sonnet: FuncPass 57.0%, SecPass 11.8% (p. 7, Table 3); 79.3% of its functionally correct solutions are insecure (p. 6). [V] (11.8/57.0 = 20.7% secure, arithmetic consistent.)
68	2. Across all 12 settings FuncPass ranges 12.9–57.0% and SecPass 3.8–12.9% (p. 7, Table 3); the authors summarise average SecPass as "only around 10%" (p. 6). [V]
69	3. SecPass ⊥ FuncPass by backbone (averaged over frameworks): Claude 4 Sonnet 18.3%, Kimi K2 22.0%, Gemini 2.5 Pro 30.4%, Gemini 3 Pro 21.4%; by framework: SWE-agent 23.3%, OpenHands 20.1%, Claude Code 17.4% (p. 6). [V] The functionally weakest model (Gemini 2.5 Pro) is the most secure on the shared subset (p. 6–7). [V]
70	4. Gemini 3 Pro more than doubles FuncPass over Gemini 2.5 Pro under SWE-agent, while SecPass ⊥ FuncPass improves only 1.3x (p. 6–7). [V]
71	5. Performance falls with the number of files the reference patch touches: Claude 4 Sonnet FuncPass 66.9% (1 file) → 39.1% (2 files) → 30.3% (>2 files); SecPass 15.4% → 4.3% → 3.0% (p. 14, Table 9). [V]
72	6. Mitigation (SWE-agent + Claude 4 Sonnet): generic 57.0 / 11.8; self-selection 50.0 / 14.5; oracle CWE hint 55.4 / 15.1 (FuncPass / SecPass) (p. 8, Table 5). [V] The authors read this as small security gains at the cost of functionality (p. 8). [A]
73	7. In self-selection the agent picks 7.2 CWE types per task on average against 1.1 ground-truth types; precision 0.086–0.114, recall 0.561–0.667 (p. 8–9, Table 6). [V]
74	8. Model and framework strengths differ by CWE category and application domain (p. 6–7, Figure 4, Table 4). [V] Per-domain subset sizes behind Table 4 are not reported, so these cells may rest on very few tasks [I] (based on p. 7).
75	
76	## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
77	- [A] Benchmark is Python-only; test outcomes are a practical proxy for security; CWE annotations and tests may be insufficient; no claim to cover all exploit modalities (p. 24).
78	- [A] Security tests from fix commits can be tied to the original implementation and reject secure alternatives; addressed by human verification and rewriting (p. 5, p. 19).
79	- [A] Fix commits may contain unrelated refactoring; addressed by ReposVul filtering, a Prospector score ≥ 65 for MoreFixes, and the verification loop (p. 15).
80	- [A] The automatic environment-building agent created operational risks (uncleaned images, over-exposed database containers), handled with command filtering (p. 18).
81	- [A] Mitigation prompts were kept deliberately simple; prompt engineering for security was not optimised (p. 19).
82	
83	## 9. Limitations we identified
84	- [I] No repeated runs, seeds or confidence intervals. With 186 tasks one task is ~0.54 pp, so many between-setting SecPass differences (e.g. 11.8 vs 12.9) are within plausible run-to-run noise. Based on the single pass@1 numbers (p. 6–7).
85	- [I] The human verification of security tests by five experts reports no inter-annotator agreement and no disagreement-resolution rule beyond "a second round of cross-checking" (p. 19). The reliability of the security oracle cannot be judged from the paper.
86	- [I] Task masks and descriptions were generated and verified by LLM agents; no human check of description quality (under-specification, hidden requirements) is reported (p. 4, p. 15–16). Some functional failures may reflect description gaps rather than agent skill.
87	- [I] Possible data contamination: tasks reconstruct historical public code and fixes in popular repositories such as django, flask and numpy (p. 13); models may have seen the secure versions. The paper does not discuss contamination of its own tasks.
88	- [I] Claude 4 Sonnet powers the environment-building agent (p. 17) and SWE-agent drives task construction (p. 4); the best-scoring setting is SWE-agent + Claude 4 Sonnet. A construction–evaluation affinity bias is possible but untested.
89	- [I] The "generic" condition already contains a security reminder (p. 7, p. 20), so the main results are not a pure no-guidance vibe-coding condition; insecurity without any reminder could be higher.
90	- [I] Security is checked by few tests per task (mean 3.5, p. 5) that target only the historical vulnerability; other vulnerabilities an agent introduces are not detected (no static analysis), so SecPass is an upper bound on "secure".
91	- [I] Funding/conflicts: work partly supported by HydroX AI (an author affiliation) with compute/credits from Modal and Google (p. 9); Gemini models are evaluated. No visible bias (Gemini 2.5 Pro scores lowest functionally), noted per the appraisal checklist.
92	
93	## 10. Threats to validity
94	- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): masks built on the vulnerable commit to avoid leaking the fix (p. 4); `.git` history removed to avoid reward hacking (p. 17) [V]. Contamination of public historical code not addressed [I]. Generic security reminder present in all main runs (p. 7) [V].
95	- External (generalisability of sample/context): Python only, 100 open-source repositories, tasks restricted to features that once had a fixed vulnerability (p. 3, p. 13, p. 24) [V]. Results describe security-sensitive feature additions to existing repositories, not whole-application generation or reconstruction from UI [I].
96	- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): FuncPass uses pre-existing upstream functional tests (mean 66.9 per task, p. 5), a fairly strong functional oracle [I]; SecPass covers only the historically known vulnerability through a few tests (p. 5, p. 24) [V]. Human-revised tests improve validity for alternative secure implementations (p. 19) [V].
97	- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): no variance, CIs or tests; per-CWE and per-domain breakdowns on small subsets (p. 7) [V]; many comparisons without correction [I].
98	- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): data, code, prompts (Appendix B–C) and step limit reported (p. 1, p. 6, p. 15–20) [V]; model versions and sampling parameters not reported.
99	
100	## 11. Future research directions
101	- Stated by authors [A]: broaden language and domain coverage; property-based and adversarial test synthesis; static/semantic program analysis; security-aware training rewards; tool use such as fuzzers, taint analysis and secret scanners (p. 24). Find strategies that improve security without disrupting functional task completion (p. 9).
102	- Suggested by us [I]: apply the same "mask and re-implement" construction to whole applications or UI-observable features, so that an original implementation and its test suite serve as a fidelity oracle for reconstruction; add static analysis to catch vulnerabilities beyond the targeted CWE; report repeated runs and annotator agreement.
103	
104	## 12. Relevance to our research
105	- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ2 (functional correctness measured with human-written tests), RQ3 (security as a quality dimension of agent/vibe-coded code), RQ4 (test-oracle design, human verification of tests, single-run pass@1), RQ5 (functional–quality divergence; no maintainability measure).
106	- How it informs our work [I]: SusVibes shows that passing functional tests says little about a second quality dimension (security): ~80% of functionally correct patches failed the security tests (p. 6). This is direct evidence that fidelity and code quality must be measured separately. Its task design (mask an existing implementation, describe it in natural language, ask an agent to re-implement it, test against the original's tests) is structurally a reconstruction-from-specification setup that could be adapted to behaviour-based reconstruction. It does not measure maintainability, UI behaviour or whole-application rebuilds, so relevance is medium.
107	
108	## 13. Evidence table (for the evidence matrix)
109	| RQ | Claim | Page | Label | Strength |

14	     status: draft (in progress) -> ready (analyst self-check passed) -> complete (critical review passed).
