input.content:
# Critical review: analyses batch B (2026-11-11)

Scope: `papers/<key>/analysis.md` for 10 keys, checked against `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index) and `metadata.json`.
Reviewer role: sceptical peer review. No analysis file was edited.

## Checks run

- `rlab cite-check 2026-11-11-ai-reverse-engineering-vibe-coding <10 analysis files>`: **OK** (59–89 citations per file, all to the paper's own key).
- `rlab validate <id> <key>`: **could not run.** It fails with `pdftotext not found` (poppler is not installed on this machine). As a fallback I read the `metadata.json` fields:
  - all 10 papers have `verification.status = verified` and `is_retracted = false`;
  - PDF identity is `match (arXiv id printed in PDF)` for 8 papers;
  - PDF identity is only `probable (title found on first pages)` for si2025benchmarking and wu2026looks. Both are ACL Anthology PDFs, and title, authors and venue footer agree with the metadata.
  - The DOI `10.18653/2026.emnlp-main.2650` (wu2026looks) looks malformed because it has no `v1/`, but it resolves at doi.org (302 to aclanthology.org). The `v1/` variant gives 404. **No problem.**
  - **Action:** install poppler and re-run `rlab validate` for all 10 keys before setting any of them to `complete`.
- Spot checks: for each paper I grepped at least 5 numbers or claims (all Key-findings numbers, the sample size and the dataset) in `fulltext.txt` and checked the cited page. Most were correct. The deviations are listed below.
- RQ links: every analysis cites RQ1–RQ5, and all five exist in `RESEARCH-QUESTIONS.md`.

## Summary

| Key | Verdict | Fixes |
|---|---|---|
| mota2026comparing | pass-with-minor-fixes | 3 |
| pan2026functional | pass-with-minor-fixes | 4 |
| si2025benchmarking | pass-with-minor-fixes | 6 |
| tran2026vibe | pass-with-minor-fixes | 6 |
| wu2026looks | pass-with-minor-fixes | 3 |
| xiao2025benchmarking | pass-with-minor-fixes | 3 |
| yang2026programbench | pass-with-minor-fixes | 2 |
| zhao2025vibe | pass-with-minor-fixes | 3 |
| zhou2025declarui | pass-with-minor-fixes | 2 |
| zhu2026understanding | pass-with-minor-fixes | 3 |

Overall quality is high:
- All 10 are full-text analyses with dense, mostly correct page refs.
- Their own critiques are paper-specific, not boilerplate (e.g. the DeclarUI ablation arithmetic, the MobileForge screenshot-only contradiction, the RAL-Bench contamination evidence).
- No invented numbers were found.

The errors are mostly mislabelled author claims, a few factual slips in evidence-table rows (these feed the evidence matrix), and version/provenance drift.

---

## mota2026comparing — pass-with-minor-fixes

1. **§9 bullet 1.**
   - Current: "a single outlier project (Lovable's wildlife-whisperer-app, p. 3) changes the tool ranking on issues and effort."
   - Problem: only half true. Replace the outlier's 59 issues with a value like its siblings (~165) and Lovable's raw issue total rises to ~496, above Replit's 463. The effort ranking does not change: each of the other two Lovable projects alone (1,782 and 1,774 min) exceeds v0's three-project total (941 min) (Table 3, p. 3; Table 6, p. 5).
   - Correct: "…changes the raw issue-count ranking (Lovable would exceed Replit), but not the remediation-effort ranking (p. 3, p. 5)."
2. **§9 bullet 4.**
   - Current: "the 'highest remediation effort' conclusion rests on a narrow base."
   - Problem: overstated, for the reason given in fix 1. The narrow part is the rule concentration (S1874, p. 6), not the project base.
   - Correct: "Lovable's effort lead is robust across 2 of 3 projects (p. 3) but is driven mainly by one rule, S1874, which per the authors accounts for more than half of the effort (p. 6); whether that rule reflects template code is unknown."
3. **§7 finding 3, label.**
   - Problem: "…and, per the authors, more than half of Lovable's effort (p. 6)" sits inside a [V] item. This share cannot be derived from any table; it is an author statement.
   - Fix: split it out as "[A] S1874 accounts for more than half of Lovable's remediation effort (p. 6)."

## pan2026functional — pass-with-minor-fixes

1. **§13 evidence row RQ3 (factual error).**
   - Current: "Reference-normalised maintainability (MI lower bound) averages ~31–33%, the weakest non-functional dimension."
   - Problem: Resource is lower than Maintainability in both tables: standard LLMs Res 31.25 vs Maint 33.45; thinking LLMs Res 28.92 vs Maint 31.38 (Tables 4–5, p. 6).
   - Correct: "…averages 33.45% (standard) and 31.38% (thinking), among the two weakest dimensions with resource usage (31.25% / 28.92%), while security averages 87.40% / 85.32% (p. 6)."
   - This row feeds the evidence matrix, so fix it before synthesis.
2. **§9 last-but-one bullet.**
   - Current: "All projects are Python libraries or CLI-style tools (p. 2), with no GUI, web front end or interactive application."
   - Problem: Table 1 includes mitmproxy (which has a web interface), Mailpile (a webmail client), glances and folium (web maps) (p. 2). The accurate limit is how they are tested, not what they are.
   - Correct: "All 38 projects are Python and are evaluated only through black-box pytest suites against their Python API/CLI surface (p. 3–4); UI behaviour is never exercised."
3. **§9 prompt-sensitivity bullet.**
   - Current: "…is not 'small' compared with the roughly 16-point spread across most models (p. 6)."
   - Problem: "most models" is undefined.
   - Correct: give the spread exactly: functional scores range 16.23–43.86% (27.6 pp) over all 16 models, and 24.37–43.86% (19.5 pp) without DeepSeek-R1 (Tables 4–5, p. 6). The +7.9 pp prompt effect is about 30–40% of the full model spread.
4. **Analyst notes.**
   - Problem 1: the note says Fig. 4 is unusable, but the text layer does show the three overall shares 44.2%, 38.6% and 17.2% (p. 7). Only the mapping of 44.2/38.6 to the two post-executability categories is ambiguous.
   - Problem 2: the PDF is arXiv **v2** (30 Mar 2026), and the version is not recorded.
   - Fix: state both.

## si2025benchmarking — pass-with-minor-fixes

1. **§7 finding 4, mislabelled.**
   - Current: "[V] Fine-tuned open models (WebSight VLM-8B, Design2Code-18B) roughly match Gemini 1.0 Pro Vision Direct (Block 55.9 / 78.5 vs 80.2…)."
   - Problem: the data contradict the claim for WebSight VLM-8B: Block-Match 55.9 vs 80.2 and Text 86.6 vs 94.6 (Table 1, p. 6). "Match" is the authors' wording (p. 5, p. 6).
   - Correct: "[A] Authors state fine-tuned models 'match Gemini direct prompting' (p. 6). [V] Design2Code-18B is close on Block (78.5 vs 80.2), but WebSight VLM-8B is far lower on Block (55.9) and Text (86.6), though higher on CLIP (87.6 vs 84.4), Position (77.3 vs 72.3) and Color (79.4 vs 66.2) (p. 6)."
2. **§7 finding 3 and §13 RQ2 row "miss 30–40% of block elements".**
   - Problem: this is the authors' paraphrase (p. 8). Block-Match is an area-weighted share that also penalises hallucinated blocks (p. 4–5), so "miss X% of elements" is not what the metric measures. Also, GPT-4o Direct at 56.6 means more than 40% unmatched area.
   - Fix: label it [A] and add "[V] HARD Block-Match ranges 56.6–75.1 across configurations (Table 3, p. 8)."
3. **§9/§10 missing validity threat (leakage in metric validation).**
   - Problem: three facts together undermine the validation.
     - The logistic regression is trained on 50 of the 100 human-annotated pages (p. 7).
     - The linear model used for simulated win rates is refit "on the same training examples" and applied "on all 484 examples", which include those training pages (p. 17).
     - The human "win + tie" rates it is compared with come from the same 100 pages (Table 8, p. 17).
   - So the r = 0.975 / τ = 0.931 agreement is not an out-of-sample validation.
   - Fix: add an [I] bullet to §9 and to §10 (Statistical/Internal). Downgrade §13 RQ4 row "Pearson r = 0.975…" (already weak) with this reason.
4. **§7 finding 2.**
   - Current: "[V] Text-augmented prompting raises Block-Match and Text for most models."
   - Problem: Table 1 shows Block-Match falling with text augmentation for GPT-4o (93.0→92.4), Claude 3 Opus (90.2→89.8) and Idefics2 (46.7→23.6) (p. 6); it rises for 4 of 7 prompted models.
   - Fix: label the "most models" summary [A] (p. 5) and state the counter-examples [V] (p. 6).
5. **§4 and §9 "Design2Code-HARD origin is inconsistent".**
   - Problem: "same filtering process" (p. 8) and "Real-World (GitHub)" source (Table 4, p. 14) are not contradictory, because the same filters can be applied to GitHub-sourced pages. The real issue is missing detail.
   - Correct: "HARD pages are sourced from GitHub (p. 14) and filtered 'using the same filtering process' (p. 8); how the GitHub pages were found and selected is not described."
6. **§5.**
   - Current: "Gemini 1.5 gave empty responses in the main experiment [V] (p. 14)."
   - Problem: the footnote says "We keep getting empty responses … while testing Gemini 1.5" (p. 14), yet Gemini 1.5 Pro/Flash results are reported for HARD (Table 3, p. 8).
   - Correct: "Gemini 1.5 is absent from the 484-page table; a footnote reports empty responses when testing it (p. 14), although Gemini 1.5 results appear on HARD (p. 8)."

## tran2026vibe — pass-with-minor-fixes

1. **§10 Reproducibility (misreading).**
   - Current: "evaluator uses LLM sampling without fixed seed ('none set in evaluator code', p. 15) [V]."
   - Problem: Table 16 reads "Model sampling override ✓ (none set in evaluator code)" (p. 15). That means no sampling-parameter override (provider defaults). Seeds are not mentioned anywhere.
   - Correct: "Evaluator uses provider-default sampling parameters, with no override set in the evaluator code (p. 15); seeds are not reported."
2. **§5, label.**
   - Current: "Main results use one generation per model per app (the variance study is the only multi-run experiment, p. 8). [V]"
   - Problem: the paper never states this. It is an inference from the SE definition across apps (p. 5) and the separate variance panel (p. 8).
   - Fix: re-label [I] and say what it is based on. The same applies to §9 bullet 4.
3. **§13 RQ2 row on difficulty and integrations (strength too high).**
   - Problem: the subgroups are tiny. In the test split, Hard = 8 apps, Email+Stripe = 7, Stripe-only = 2 and Email-only = 4 (Tables 5–6, p. 6). "6.0% hard" and "13.5% email + Stripe" rest on 7–8 apps each.
   - Fix: add the n to the claim and set strength to **weak**. Note in §9 that the subgroup cells are too small for comparison.
4. **Frontmatter `main_finding`.**
   - Current: "evaluator choice changes step-level agreement from 31.8% to 93.6%."
   - Problem: 93.6% is human–human agreement (Reviewer A vs B, Table 10, p. 9), not an evaluator-choice effect. The abstract uses this framing (p. 1), but it is the authors' framing.
   - Correct: "…judge–human step agreement ranges 31.8–87.5% depending on the evaluator model (mean 36.1% for GPT-5.2 vs 86.4% for Claude Sonnet 4.5, p. 9)."
5. **Provenance / version.**
   - Problem 1: the header says "(published)" in ACM proceedings, but the analysed PDF is arXiv v3 (13 May 2026) with no ACM header, and all page refs are arXiv pages (Analyst notes say so).
   - Problem 2: `metadata.json`'s abstract says "50 **public** validation" while the PDF abstract says "50 **private** validation" (p. 1). This is version drift, and it bears on the private/public inconsistency the analysis already flags (§4, §9).
   - Fix: add both facts to the Venue note. Try `rlab fetch` for the ACM version; if no open-access copy exists, keep arXiv v3 and say so explicitly in the header.
6. **§9 bullet 2 (over-confident interpretation).**
   - Current: "…implies GPT-5.2 labels largely the opposite way … which points to a systematic problem."
   - Problem: speculative. Keep it, but hedge it, and cite the one supporting cue in the paper: GPT-5.2 evaluation cost is $0.093 per workflow vs $1.48 for Sonnet 4.6 (p. 9). That is consistent with very short or terminated runs being scored as fails (p. 5), but the paper does not show this.

## wu2026looks — pass-with-minor-fixes

1. **§6 / §9 human validation of the visual judge.**
   - Current: "Number and expertise of human raters and their agreement — not reported."
   - Problem: the paper says "**We** labelled 55 scenarios with a blinded ranking interface" (p. 13). The raters are therefore the authors, which is a missing independence threat.
   - Fix: add "[I] Human reference labels were produced by the authors themselves (p. 13), not independent raters." Put this in §9 and §10 (Internal).
2. **§4 page refs.**
   - Problem: the annotation-accuracy figures (96.8/94.3; 74.1/83.9; 64.7/76.5) are cited "(pp. 3, 9, 15)". Page 9 does not contain them; they are on p. 3 and in Table 9, p. 15.
   - Fix: change the refs to (p. 3, p. 15).
3. **§6 cross-judge, label.**
   - Problem: "no self-preference observed [V] (p. 13)" is a qualitative author statement with no numbers given ("slightly lower normalised Borda").
   - Fix: re-label [A].
   - Also add to §10: Gemini 2.5 Pro is both the judge and an evaluated model. The only self-preference check is against one other judge on 139 scenarios from 5 apps (p. 13).

## xiao2025benchmarking — pass-with-minor-fixes

1. **Header author list incomplete.**
   - Problem: the analysis lists 6 authors. `metadata.json` and the PDF (p. 1) list 9.
   - Correct: "Xiao, Jingyu; Wan, Yuxuan; Huo, Yintong; Wang, Zixin; Xu, Xinyi; Wang, Wenxuan; Xu, Zhiyao; Wang, Yuhang; Lyu, Michael R."
2. **§13 RQ2 row.**
   - Current: "Best human Usability Rate 81% (GPT-4o Mark); Claude 66–77%; Qwen-3B 17–19% on 374 interactions."
   - Problem: the number of interactions that were human-evaluated is not reported. The analysis's own §6 says "Number of items in the human evaluations — not reported."
   - Fix: delete "on 374 interactions" and add "(number of evaluated items not reported, p. 6)".
3. **§7 finding 7.**
   - Current: "combining visual and human-written text descriptions beats either modality alone for GPT-4o."
   - Problem: Table VIII has a counter-example. Under the Mark prompt, SSIM for V+T is 0.4336, below V (0.4520) and T (0.4454) (p. 10). The authors' claim that V+T "consistently outperforms single-modality inputs across all prompt types" (p. 10) is therefore not fully supported, on 10 pages only.
   - Fix: add this as [V] and mark the authors' generalisation [A]. Add it to §9 alongside the FAP contradiction.

## yang2026programbench — pass-with-minor-fixes

1. **§13 RQ4 row.**
   - Current: "With internet access, 20–36% of runs by stronger models **cheated**…"
   - Problem: the paper reports tasks **flagged** by majority vote of 9 LM judges, and says judges disagree on 40–57% of tasks for these models (p. 6), with κ = 0.57 (p. 17). "Cheated" overstates it.
   - Correct: "20–36% of tasks were flagged as cheating by a 9-judge majority vote; judges disagreed on 40–57% of tasks (p. 6; p. 17)."
2. **§7 finding 9.**
   - Current: "Probing the executable is the second-largest action category, at 22.6–34.1% of turns (p. 10)."
   - Problem: the paper states this for the four models in the trajectory analysis ("for all four", p. 10), not for all 9.
   - Fix: add the scope.

## zhao2025vibe — pass-with-minor-fixes

## Cross-paper observations

1. **Same-family construction or judging, with same-family winners (a recurring threat).**
   - ProgramBench: tests were written by Claude Sonnet 4.5 with source access, and Claude models top the leaderboard [@yang2026programbench, p. 3; p. 31].

   - MobileForge: Gemini 2.5 Pro is both judge and candidate [@wu2026looks, p. 6].
   - SusVibes: the environment builder is Claude 4 Sonnet, and SWE-agent + Claude 4 Sonnet is best on FuncPass [@zhao2025vibe, p. 7; p. 17].
   - Only MobileForge tests self-preference, and only qualitatively [@wu2026looks, p. 13].

2. **Does iterative feedback help? There is an apparent tension.**
   - One-shot self-repair, environment repair and planning did not raise functional scores and lowered non-functional quality [@pan2026functional, p. 8].
   - Browser self-testing correlates with accuracy (r = 0.72 across 16 models) [@tran2026vibe, p. 7].
   - Compiler-feedback loops raise compile success, 74% to 98% [@zhou2025declarui, p. 9], and make build success saturate at 100% [@wu2026looks, p. 12].

3. **Reasoning or "thinking" effort.**
   - "Thinking" models are not consistently better and average slightly below standard ones [@pan2026functional, p. 6].
   - Higher reasoning effort clearly helps GPT and Gemini 3.1 Pro on Vibe Code Bench (20-app subset) [@tran2026vibe, p. 7].
   - These differ in setting (single pass vs agentic) and are not a direct contradiction, but should be noted.
4. **Code size and structure point in different directions depending on the baseline.**
   - Rebuilt CLIs are smaller and more monolithic than the human originals [@yang2026programbench, p. 9].
   - Among models, the visual leader writes 2.2× more code with larger files [@wu2026looks, p. 6].
   - Replit produces about 60% duplicated lines [@mota2026comparing, p. 4].
   - MetaGPT needed explicit modularity prompts to avoid monolithic God classes [@zhu2026understanding, p. 5].
   - "More code is worse" is not established. Both mota (per KLOC) and zhu (raw counts, ρ = 0.94 with TLoC) treat smell counts as size-driven, but only mota normalises.

   - mota2026comparing relies on SonarQube alone [@mota2026comparing, p. 2].
   - When synthesising RQ3, check molison2025llm's analysis for this disagreement about measurement validity.
6. **Possible data overlap.**
   - Interaction2Code takes 100 of its 127 pages from the C4 validation set, using Design2Code's filtering [@xiao2025benchmarking, p. 2].
   - Design2Code's 484 pages also come from the C4 validation set [@si2025benchmarking, p. 2].
   - The two benchmarks may share source pages, so they are not fully independent evidence on screenshot-to-code fidelity.
   - Both reuse the same Position metric (1 − max(|Δx|, |Δy|)) [@si2025benchmarking, p. 4; @xiao2025benchmarking, p. 4].
7. **Version drift.**
   - Four analyses cite a published DOI but analyse an arXiv version: tran2026vibe (v3), xiao2025benchmarking (v3, later than ASE 2025), zhou2025declarui (v1, earlier than PACMSE), zhu2026understanding (v1, with a different title).
   - zhao2025vibe has the opposite problem: published, but metadata says preprint.
   - Page refs follow the arXiv PDFs in all four cases, so quotes in reports must cite the PDF actually held.
8. **Model overlap allows a weak consistency check.**
   - Claude Opus 4.6 is top-tier in three independent benchmarks [@tran2026vibe, p. 6; @yang2026programbench, p. 31; @wu2026looks, p. 7].
   - GPT-5.2 appears in pan (41.81% functional) and tran (53.50%), and is also the worst-aligned judge in tran [@pan2026functional, p. 6; @tran2026vibe, p. 9].
   - [I] Rankings agree in broad terms, but the metrics are not comparable, so absolute numbers must not be pooled.
9. **Contamination handling is uneven.**
   - Only Interaction2Code runs an explicit check, a BLEU similarity to the original HTML [@xiao2025benchmarking, p. 5], and the analysis rightly calls it weak.
   - ProgramBench uses a different-language ablation [@yang2026programbench, p. 6].
   - RAL-Bench acknowledges exposure [@pan2026functional, p. 2].
   - MobileForge, DeclarUI, SusVibes and Design2Code do not discuss contamination of their own data, even though all use popular public apps or pages.
   - This is a candidate RQ4/RQ5 gap and needs a novelty check before it can be claimed.

# Critical review: analyses batch B (2026-11-11)

Scope: `papers/<key>/analysis.md` for 10 keys, checked against `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index) and `metadata.json`.
Reviewer role: sceptical peer review. No analysis file was edited.

## Checks run

- `rlab cite-check 2026-11-11-ai-reverse-engineering-vibe-coding <10 analysis files>`: **OK** (59–89 citations per file, all to the paper's own key).
- `rlab validate <id> <key>`: **could not run.** It fails with `pdftotext not found` (poppler is not installed on this machine). As a fallback I read the `metadata.json` fields:
  - all 10 papers have `verification.status = verified` and `is_retracted = false`;
  - PDF identity is `match (arXiv id printed in PDF)` for 8 papers;
  - PDF identity is only `probable (title found on first pages)` for si2025benchmarking and wu2026looks. Both are ACL Anthology PDFs, and title, authors and venue footer agree with the metadata.
  - The DOI `10.18653/2026.emnlp-main.2650` (wu2026looks) looks malformed because it has no `v1/`, but it resolves at doi.org (302 to aclanthology.org). The `v1/` variant gives 404. **No problem.**
  - **Action:** install poppler and re-run `rlab validate` for all 10 keys before setting any of them to `complete`.
- Spot checks: for each paper I grepped at least 5 numbers or claims (all Key-findings numbers, the sample size and the dataset) in `fulltext.txt` and checked the cited page. Most were correct. The deviations are listed below.
- RQ links: every analysis cites RQ1–RQ5, and all five exist in `RESEARCH-QUESTIONS.md`.

## Summary

| Key | Verdict | Fixes |
|---|---|---|
| mota2026comparing | pass-with-minor-fixes | 3 |
| pan2026functional | pass-with-minor-fixes | 4 |
| si2025benchmarking | pass-with-minor-fixes | 6 |
| tran2026vibe | pass-with-minor-fixes | 6 |
| wu2026looks | pass-with-minor-fixes | 3 |

Overall quality is high:
- All 10 are full-text analyses with dense, mostly correct page refs.

PACMSE is an ACM open-access journal, so a legal published copy is probably available.
   - Fix: try `rlab fetch` for the ACM version, re-check Tables 1–3, and record any differences in a Revision section.
2. **§9 ablation bullet (sharpen).**
   - Problem: the bullet should add the decisive detail. In the ablation table, the "Full" row's CLIP/SSIM (0.90/0.72, p. 10) differ from the 50-app values (0.88/0.68, p. 9), while PCR/ACIC/CSR are identical (96.8 / 0.22 / 98.0).
   - Fix: add that detail and conclude "This strongly suggests the visual metrics were recomputed on 13 apps but PCR/ACIC/CSR were copied from the 50-app run (p. 9–10)."

## zhu2026understanding — pass-with-minor-fixes

1. **§7 finding 5, label.**
   - Current: "[V] … most prevalent smells were TMB, RFC, PAU, SF, UD, **across all stages and scenarios**."
   - Problem: Figure 1 pools all repositories, and the analyst read only its caption (Analyst notes). "Consistent appearance across all stages and scenarios" is the authors' text (p. 7).
   - Fix: keep [V] for the ranking by mean from the Figure 1 caption (p. 8) and label the "all stages and scenarios" part [A] (p. 7).
2. **Provenance.**
   - Problem 1: the arXiv PDF title ("AI-Generated Smells: An Analysis of Code and Architecture in LLM- and Agent-Driven Development") differs from the metadata title.
   - Problem 2: `rlab`'s identity "match" relies on the arXiv id that the metadata itself links to the ACM DOI.
   - Problem 3: `oa_pdf_url` points to the ACM DL, but the text was taken from arXiv.
   - Fix: fetch the ACM version (listed as OA) and confirm it is the same work. If it cannot be fetched, keep the analysis but mark the DOI–PDF link as "probable".
3. **§4 / frontmatter "20 implied".**
   - Problem: this can be supported. The reported Spearman p-values (ρ = 0.53, p = 0.017; ρ = 0.59, p = 0.007; Table 3, p. 9) are consistent with n ≈ 20.
   - Fix: add as [I]. Also keep the point that each stage is likely an independent generation, since the stage prompts are self-contained (p. 5).

---

## Cross-paper observations

1. **Same-family construction or judging, with same-family winners (a recurring threat).**
   - ProgramBench: tests were written by Claude Sonnet 4.5 with source access, and Claude models top the leaderboard [@yang2026programbench, p. 3; p. 31].
   - Vibe Code Bench: Claude Sonnet 4.5 is the judge, and Anthropic and OpenAI models lead; the specs were drafted by GPT-5 and GPT-5.3-Codex is first [@tran2026vibe, p. 3; p. 4; p. 6].
   - MobileForge: Gemini 2.5 Pro is both judge and candidate [@wu2026looks, p. 6].
   - SusVibes: the environment builder is Claude 4 Sonnet, and SWE-agent + Claude 4 Sonnet is best on FuncPass [@zhao2025vibe, p. 7; p. 17].
   - Only MobileForge tests self-preference, and only qualitatively [@wu2026looks, p. 13].
   - The evidence matrix should list this as a shared RQ4 weakness, not repeat it per paper.
2. **Does iterative feedback help? There is an apparent tension.**
   - One-shot self-repair, environment repair and planning did not raise functional scores and lowered non-functional quality [@pan2026functional, p. 8].
   - Browser self-testing correlates with accuracy (r = 0.72 across 16 models) [@tran2026vibe, p. 7].
   - Compiler-feedback loops raise compile success, 74% to 98% [@zhou2025declarui, p. 9], and make build success saturate at 100% [@wu2026looks, p. 12].
   - [I] Possible reconciliation: one-shot interventions vs multi-step agentic loops, and different outcome metrics (non-functional quality vs workflow pass / compilation). Record both sides under "Contradictions" in the evidence matrix (standards §6). Do not pick a side.
3. **Reasoning or "thinking" effort.**
   - "Thinking" models are not consistently better and average slightly below standard ones [@pan2026functional, p. 6].
   - Higher reasoning effort clearly helps GPT and Gemini 3.1 Pro on Vibe Code Bench (20-app subset) [@tran2026vibe, p. 7].
   - These differ in setting (single pass vs agentic) and are not a direct contradiction, but should be noted.
4. **Code size and structure point in different directions depending on the baseline.**
   - Rebuilt CLIs are smaller and more monolithic than the human originals [@yang2026programbench, p. 9].
   - Among models, the visual leader writes 2.2× more code with larger files [@wu2026looks, p. 6].
   - Replit produces about 60% duplicated lines [@mota2026comparing, p. 4].
   - MetaGPT needed explicit modularity prompts to avoid monolithic God classes [@zhu2026understanding, p. 5].
   - "More code is worse" is not established. Both mota (per KLOC) and zhu (raw counts, ρ = 0.94 with TLoC) treat smell counts as size-driven, but only mota normalises.
5. **SonarQube vs PyExamine, and the molison2025llm link.**
   - zhu2026understanding argues that SonarQube issue counts conflate linting with structural smells, and positions itself against Santa Molison et al. (= project key `molison2025llm`) [@zhu2026understanding, p. 2].
   - mota2026comparing relies on SonarQube alone [@mota2026comparing, p. 2].
   - When synthesising RQ3, check molison2025llm's analysis for this disagreement about measurement validity.
6. **Possible data overlap.**
   - Interaction2Code takes 100 of its 127 pages from the C4 validation set, using Design2Code's filtering [@xiao2025benchmarking, p. 2].
   - Design2Code's 484 pages also come from the C4 validation set [@si2025benchmarking, p. 2].
   - The two benchmarks may share source pages, so they are not fully independent evidence on screenshot-to-code fidelity.
   - Both reuse the same Position metric (1 − max(|Δx|, |Δy|)) [@si2025benchmarking, p. 4; @xiao2025benchmarking, p. 4].
7. **Version drift.**
   - Four analyses cite a published DOI but analyse an arXiv version: tran2026vibe (v3), xiao2025benchmarking (v3, later than ASE 2025), zhou2025declarui (v1, earlier than PACMSE), zhu2026understanding (v1, with a different title).
   - zhao2025vibe has the opposite problem: published, but metadata says preprint.
   - Page refs follow the arXiv PDFs in all four cases, so quotes in reports must cite the PDF actually held.
8. **Model overlap allows a weak consistency check.**
   - Claude Opus 4.6 is top-tier in three independent benchmarks [@tran2026vibe, p. 6; @yang2026programbench, p. 31; @wu2026looks, p. 7].
   - GPT-5.2 appears in pan (41.81% functional) and tran (53.50%), and is also the worst-aligned judge in tran [@pan2026functional, p. 6; @tran2026vibe, p. 9].
   - [I] Rankings agree in broad terms, but the metrics are not comparable, so absolute numbers must not be pooled.
9. **Contamination handling is uneven.**
   - Only Interaction2Code runs an explicit check, a BLEU similarity to the original HTML [@xiao2025benchmarking, p. 5], and the analysis rightly calls it weak.
   - ProgramBench uses a different-language ablation [@yang2026programbench, p. 6].
   - RAL-Bench acknowledges exposure [@pan2026functional, p. 2].
   - MobileForge, DeclarUI, SusVibes and Design2Code do not discuss contamination of their own data, even though all use popular public apps or pages.
   - This is a candidate RQ4/RQ5 gap and needs a novelty check before it can be claimed.

# Critical review: analyses batch B (2026-11-11)

Scope: `papers/<key>/analysis.md` for 10 keys, checked against `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index) and `metadata.json`.
Reviewer role: sceptical peer review. No analysis file was edited.

## Checks run

- `rlab cite-check 2026-11-11-ai-reverse-engineering-vibe-coding <10 analysis files>`: **OK** (59–89 citations per file, all to the paper's own key).
- `rlab validate <id> <key>`: **could not run.** It fails with `pdftotext not found` (poppler is not installed on this machine). As a fallback I read the `metadata.json` fields:
  - all 10 papers have `verification.status = verified` and `is_retracted = false`;
  - PDF identity is `match (arXiv id printed in PDF)` for 8 papers;
  - PDF identity is only `probable (title found on first pages)` for si2025benchmarking and wu2026looks. Both are ACL Anthology PDFs, and title, authors and venue footer agree with the metadata.
  - The DOI `10.18653/2026.emnlp-main.2650` (wu2026looks) looks malformed because it has no `v1/`, but it resolves at doi.org (302 to aclanthology.org). The `v1/` variant gives 404. **No problem.**
  - **Action:** install poppler and re-run `rlab validate` for all 10 keys before setting any of them to `complete`.
- Spot checks: for each paper I grepped at least 5 numbers or claims (all Key-findings numbers, the sample size and the dataset) in `fulltext.txt` and checked the cited page. Most were correct. The deviations are listed below.
- RQ links: every analysis cites RQ1–RQ5, and all five exist in `RESEARCH-QUESTIONS.md`.

## Summary

| Key | Verdict | Fixes |
|---|---|---|
| mota2026comparing | pass-with-minor-fixes | 3 |
| pan2026functional | pass-with-minor-fixes | 4 |
| si2025benchmarking | pass-with-minor-fixes | 6 |
| tran2026vibe | pass-with-minor-fixes | 6 |
| wu2026looks | pass-with-minor-fixes | 3 |
| xiao2025benchmarking | pass-with-minor-fixes | 3 |
| yang2026programbench | pass-with-minor-fixes | 2 |
| zhao2025vibe | pass-with-minor-fixes | 3 |
| zhou2025declarui | pass-with-minor-fixes | 2 |
| zhu2026understanding | pass-with-minor-fixes | 3 |

Overall quality is high:
- All 10 are full-text analyses with dense, mostly correct page refs.
- Their own critiques are paper-specific, not boilerplate (e.g. the DeclarUI ablation arithmetic, the MobileForge screenshot-only contradiction, the RAL-Bench contamination evidence).
- No invented numbers were found.

The errors are mostly mislabelled author claims, a few factual slips in evidence-table rows (these feed the evidence matrix), and version/provenance drift.

---

## mota2026comparing — pass-with-minor-fixes

1. **§9 bullet 1.**
   - Current: "a single outlier project (Lovable's wildlife-whisperer-app, p. 3) changes the tool ranking on issues and effort."
   - Problem: only half true. Replace the outlier's 59 issues with a value like its siblings (~165) and Lovable's raw issue total rises to ~496, above Replit's 463. The effort ranking does not change: each of the other two Lovable projects alone (1,782 and 1,774 min) exceeds v0's three-project total (941 min) (Table 3, p. 3; Table 6, p. 5).
   - Correct: "…changes the raw issue-count ranking (Lovable would exceed Replit), but not the remediation-effort ranking (p. 3, p. 5)."
2. **§9 bullet 4.**
   - Current: "the 'highest remediation effort' conclusion rests on a narrow base."
   - Problem: overstated, for the reason given in fix 1. The narrow part is the rule concentration (S1874, p. 6), not the project base.
   - Correct: "Lovable's effort lead is robust across 2 of 3 projects (p. 3) but is driven mainly by one rule, S1874, which per the authors accounts for more than half of the effort (p. 6); whether that rule reflects template code is unknown."
3. **§7 finding 3, label.**
   - Problem: "…and, per the authors, more than half of Lovable's effort (p. 6)" sits inside a [V] item. This share cannot be derived from any table; it is an author statement.
   - Fix: split it out as "[A] S1874 accounts for more than half of Lovable's remediation effort (p. 6)."

## pan2026functional — pass-with-minor-fixes

1. **§13 evidence row RQ3 (factual error).**
   - Current: "Reference-normalised maintainability (MI lower bound) averages ~31–33%, the weakest non-functional dimension."
   - Problem: Resource is lower than Maintainability in both tables: standard LLMs Res 31.25 vs Maint 33.45; thinking LLMs Res 28.92 vs Maint 31.38 (Tables 4–5, p. 6).
   - Correct: "…averages 33.45% (standard) and 31.38% (thinking), among the two weakest dimensions with resource usage (31.25% / 28.92%), while security averages 87.40% / 85.32% (p. 6)."
   - This row feeds the evidence matrix, so fix it before synthesis.
2. **§9 last-but-one bullet.**
   - Current: "All projects are Python libraries or CLI-style tools (p. 2), with no GUI, web front end or interactive application."
   - Problem: Table 1 includes mitmproxy (which has a web interface), Mailpile (a webmail client), glances and folium (web maps) (p. 2). The accurate limit is how they are tested, not what they are.
   - Correct: "All 38 projects are Python and are evaluated only through black-box pytest suites against their Python API/CLI surface (p. 3–4); UI behaviour is never exercised."
3. **§9 prompt-sensitivity bullet.**
   - Current: "…is not 'small' compared with the roughly 16-point spread across most models (p. 6)."
   - Problem: "most models" is undefined.
   - Correct: give the spread exactly: functional scores range 16.23–43.86% (27.6 pp) over all 16 models, and 24.37–43.86% (19.5 pp) without DeepSeek-R1 (Tables 4–5, p. 6). The +7.9 pp prompt effect is about 30–40% of the full model spread.
4. **Analyst notes.**
   - Problem 1: the note says Fig. 4 is unusable, but the text layer does show the three overall shares 44.2%, 38.6% and 17.2% (p. 7). Only the mapping of 44.2/38.6 to the two post-executability categories is ambiguous.
   - Problem 2: the PDF is arXiv **v2** (30 Mar 2026), and the version is not recorded.
   - Fix: state both.

## si2025benchmarking — pass-with-minor-fixes

1. **§7 finding 4, mislabelled.**
   - Current: "[V] Fine-tuned open models (WebSight VLM-8B, Design2Code-18B) roughly match Gemini 1.0 Pro Vision Direct (Block 55.9 / 78.5 vs 80.2…)."
   - Problem: the data contradict the claim for WebSight VLM-8B: Block-Match 55.9 vs 80.2 and Text 86.6 vs 94.6 (Table 1, p. 6). "Match" is the authors' wording (p. 5, p. 6).
   - Correct: "[A] Authors state fine-tuned models 'match Gemini direct prompting' (p. 6). [V] Design2Code-18B is close on Block (78.5 vs 80.2), but WebSight VLM-8B is far lower on Block (55.9) and Text (86.6), though higher on CLIP (87.6 vs 84.4), Position (77.3 vs 72.3) and Color (79.4 vs 66.2) (p. 6)."
2. **§7 finding 3 and §13 RQ2 row "miss 30–40% of block elements".**
   - Problem: this is the authors' paraphrase (p. 8). Block-Match is an area-weighted share that also penalises hallucinated blocks (p. 4–5), so "miss X% of elements" is not what the metric measures. Also, GPT-4o Direct at 56.6 means more than 40% unmatched area.
   - Fix: label it [A] and add "[V] HARD Block-Match ranges 56.6–75.1 across configurations (Table 3, p. 8)."
3. **§9/§10 missing validity threat (leakage in metric validation).**
   - Problem: three facts together undermine the validation.
     - The logistic regression is trained on 50 of the 100 human-annotated pages (p. 7).
     - The linear model used for simulated win rates is refit "on the same training examples" and applied "on all 484 examples", which include those training pages (p. 17).
     - The human "win + tie" rates it is compared with come from the same 100 pages (Table 8, p. 17).
   - So the r = 0.975 / τ = 0.931 agreement is not an out-of-sample validation.
   - Fix: add an [I] bullet to §9 and to §10 (Statistical/Internal). Downgrade §13 RQ4 row "Pearson r = 0.975…" (already weak) with this reason.
4. **§7 finding 2.**
   - Current: "[V] Text-augmented prompting raises Block-Match and Text for most models."
   - Problem: Table 1 shows Block-Match falling with text augmentation for GPT-4o (93.0→92.4), Claude 3 Opus (90.2→89.8) and Idefics2 (46.7→23.6) (p. 6); it rises for 4 of 7 prompted models.
   - Fix: label the "most models" summary [A] (p. 5) and state the counter-examples [V] (p. 6).
5. **§4 and §9 "Design2Code-HARD origin is inconsistent".**
   - Problem: "same filtering process" (p. 8) and "Real-World (GitHub)" source (Table 4, p. 14) are not contradictory, because the same filters can be applied to GitHub-sourced pages. The real issue is missing detail.
   - Correct: "HARD pages are sourced from GitHub (p. 14) and filtered 'using the same filtering process' (p. 8); how the GitHub pages were found and selected is not described."
6. **§5.**
   - Current: "Gemini 1.5 gave empty responses in the main experiment [V] (p. 14)."
   - Problem: the footnote says "We keep getting empty responses … while testing Gemini 1.5" (p. 14), yet Gemini 1.5 Pro/Flash results are reported for HARD (Table 3, p. 8).
   - Correct: "Gemini 1.5 is absent from the 484-page table; a footnote reports empty responses when testing it (p. 14), although Gemini 1.5 results appear on HARD (p. 8)."

## tran2026vibe — pass-with-minor-fixes

1. **§10 Reproducibility (misreading).**
   - Current: "evaluator uses LLM sampling without fixed seed ('none set in evaluator code', p. 15) [V]."
   - Problem: Table 16 reads "Model sampling override ✓ (none set in evaluator code)" (p. 15). That means no sampling-parameter override (provider defaults). Seeds are not mentioned anywhere.
   - Correct: "Evaluator uses provider-default sampling parameters, with no override set in the evaluator code (p. 15); seeds are not reported."
2. **§5, label.**
   - Current: "Main results use one generation per model per app (the variance study is the only multi-run experiment, p. 8). [V]"
   - Problem: the paper never states this. It is an inference from the SE definition across apps (p. 5) and the separate variance panel (p. 8).
   - Fix: re-label [I] and say what it is based on. The same applies to §9 bullet 4.
3. **§13 RQ2 row on difficulty and integrations (strength too high).**
   - Problem: the subgroups are tiny. In the test split, Hard = 8 apps, Email+Stripe = 7, Stripe-only = 2 and Email-only = 4 (Tables 5–6, p. 6). "6.0% hard" and "13.5% email + Stripe" rest on 7–8 apps each.

4. **Frontmatter `main_finding`.**
   - Current: "evaluator choice changes step-level agreement from 31.8% to 93.6%."

   - Problem 2: `rlab`'s identity "match" relies on the arXiv id that the metadata itself links to the ACM DOI.
   - Problem 3: `oa_pdf_url` points to the ACM DL, but the text was taken from arXiv.
   - Fix: fetch the ACM version (listed as OA) and confirm it is the same work. If it cannot be fetched, keep the analysis but mark the DOI–PDF link as "probable".
3. **§4 / frontmatter "20 implied".**
   - Problem: this can be supported. The reported Spearman p-values (ρ = 0.53, p = 0.017; ρ = 0.59, p = 0.007; Table 3, p. 9) are consistent with n ≈ 20.
   - Fix: add as [I]. Also keep the point that each stage is likely an independent generation, since the stage prompts are self-contained (p. 5).

---

## Cross-paper observations

1. **Same-family construction or judging, with same-family winners (a recurring threat).**
   - ProgramBench: tests were written by Claude Sonnet 4.5 with source access, and Claude models top the leaderboard [@yang2026programbench, p. 3; p. 31].
   - Vibe Code Bench: Claude Sonnet 4.5 is the judge, and Anthropic and OpenAI models lead; the specs were drafted by GPT-5 and GPT-5.3-Codex is first [@tran2026vibe, p. 3; p. 4; p. 6].
   - MobileForge: Gemini 2.5 Pro is both judge and candidate [@wu2026looks, p. 6].
   - SusVibes: the environment builder is Claude 4 Sonnet, and SWE-agent + Claude 4 Sonnet is best on FuncPass [@zhao2025vibe, p. 7; p. 17].
   - Only MobileForge tests self-preference, and only qualitatively [@wu2026looks, p. 13].
   - The evidence matrix should list this as a shared RQ4 weakness, not repeat it per paper.
2. **Does iterative feedback help? There is an apparent tension.**
   - One-shot self-repair, environment repair and planning did not raise functional scores and lowered non-functional quality [@pan2026functional, p. 8].
   - Browser self-testing correlates with accuracy (r = 0.72 across 16 models) [@tran2026vibe, p. 7].
   - Compiler-feedback loops raise compile success, 74% to 98% [@zhou2025declarui, p. 9], and make build success saturate at 100% [@wu2026looks, p. 12].
   - [I] Possible reconciliation: one-shot interventions vs multi-step agentic loops, and different outcome metrics (non-functional quality vs workflow pass / compilation). Record both sides under "Contradictions" in the evidence matrix (standards §6). Do not pick a side.
3. **Reasoning or "thinking" effort.**
   - "Thinking" models are not consistently better and average slightly below standard ones [@pan2026functional, p. 6].
   - Higher reasoning effort clearly helps GPT and Gemini 3.1 Pro on Vibe Code Bench (20-app subset) [@tran2026vibe, p. 7].
   - These differ in setting (single pass vs agentic) and are not a direct contradiction, but should be noted.
4. **Code size and structure point in different directions depending on the baseline.**
   - Rebuilt CLIs are smaller and more monolithic than the human originals [@yang2026programbench, p. 9].
   - Among models, the visual leader writes 2.2× more code with larger files [@wu2026looks, p. 6].
   - Replit produces about 60% duplicated lines [@mota2026comparing, p. 4].
   - MetaGPT needed explicit modularity prompts to avoid monolithic God classes [@zhu2026understanding, p. 5].
   - "More code is worse" is not established. Both mota (per KLOC) and zhu (raw counts, ρ = 0.94 with TLoC) treat smell counts as size-driven, but only mota normalises.
5. **SonarQube vs PyExamine, and the molison2025llm link.**
   - zhu2026understanding argues that SonarQube issue counts conflate linting with structural smells, and positions itself against Santa Molison et al. (= project key `molison2025llm`) [@zhu2026understanding, p. 2].
   - mota2026comparing relies on SonarQube alone [@mota2026comparing, p. 2].
   - When synthesising RQ3, check molison2025llm's analysis for this disagreement about measurement validity.
6. **Possible data overlap.**
   - Interaction2Code takes 100 of its 127 pages from the C4 validation set, using Design2Code's filtering [@xiao2025benchmarking, p. 2].
   - Design2Code's 484 pages also come from the C4 validation set [@si2025benchmarking, p. 2].
   - The two benchmarks may share source pages, so they are not fully independent evidence on screenshot-to-code fidelity.
   - Both reuse the same Position metric (1 − max(|Δx|, |Δy|)) [@si2025benchmarking, p. 4; @xiao2025benchmarking, p. 4].
7. **Version drift.**
   - Four analyses cite a published DOI but analyse an arXiv version: tran2026vibe (v3), xiao2025benchmarking (v3, later than ASE 2025), zhou2025declarui (v1, earlier than PACMSE), zhu2026understanding (v1, with a different title).
   - zhao2025vibe has the opposite problem: published, but metadata says preprint.
   - Page refs follow the arXiv PDFs in all four cases, so quotes in reports must cite the PDF actually held.
8. **Model overlap allows a weak consistency check.**
   - Claude Opus 4.6 is top-tier in three independent benchmarks [@tran2026vibe, p. 6; @yang2026programbench, p. 31; @wu2026looks, p. 7].
   - GPT-5.2 appears in pan (41.81% functional) and tran (53.50%), and is also the worst-aligned judge in tran [@pan2026functional, p. 6; @tran2026vibe, p. 9].
   - [I] Rankings agree in broad terms, but the metrics are not comparable, so absolute numbers must not be pooled.
9. **Contamination handling is uneven.**
   - Only Interaction2Code runs an explicit check, a BLEU similarity to the original HTML [@xiao2025benchmarking, p. 5], and the analysis rightly calls it weak.
   - ProgramBench uses a different-language ablation [@yang2026programbench, p. 6].
   - RAL-Bench acknowledges exposure [@pan2026functional, p. 2].
   - MobileForge, DeclarUI, SusVibes and Design2Code do not discuss contamination of their own data, even though all use popular public apps or pages.
   - This is a candidate RQ4/RQ5 gap and needs a novelty check before it can be claimed.

The fixes are mislabelled author claims, a few factual slips in evidence-table rows (which feed the evidence matrix), and version or provenance drift.

`rlab cite-check` passes for all 10 analyses and for the report itself. I could not run `rlab validate`: it fails with `pdftotext not found` because poppler is not installed. Instead I checked the provenance fields in `metadata.json`: all 10 are verified and none is retracted. Two have PDF identity rated only "probable" (si2025benchmarking, wu2026looks). Install poppler and re-run `rlab validate` before setting any of these to complete.

| Key | Verdict | Fixes |
|---|---|---|
| mota2026comparing | pass-with-minor-fixes | 3 |
| pan2026functional | pass-with-minor-fixes | 4 |
| si2025benchmarking | pass-with-minor-fixes | 6 |
| tran2026vibe | pass-with-minor-fixes | 6 |
| wu2026looks | pass-with-minor-fixes | 3 |
| xiao2025benchmarking | pass-with-minor-fixes | 3 |
| yang2026programbench | pass-with-minor-fixes | 2 |
| zhao2025vibe | pass-with-minor-fixes | 3 |
| zhou2025declarui | pass-with-minor-fixes | 2 |
| zhu2026understanding | pass-with-minor-fixes | 3 |

**Most serious issues:**
1. **pan2026functional, evidence row RQ3 (factual error):** it calls maintainability "the weakest non-functional dimension". Resource usage is lower in both tables: 31.25 vs 33.45 for standard models and 28.92 vs 31.38 for thinking models (p. 6). This row would go straight into the evidence matrix.
2. **si2025benchmarking:**
   - Finding 4 is labelled [V] ("fine-tuned models roughly match Gemini"), but WebSight VLM-8B scores 55.9 vs 80.2 on Block-Match (p. 6). It should be [A] with the contradiction noted.
   - A leakage threat is missing: the metric-to-human regression was fit on 50 of the same 100 annotated pages it is compared against, and the simulated win rates include those training pages (p. 7, p. 17). So r = 0.975 is not an out-of-sample validation.
3. **tran2026vibe:**
   - "No fixed seed (p. 15)" is a misreading. Table 16 says no sampling-parameter override; seeds are not mentioned.
   - "One generation per model per app" is labelled [V] but is only an inference, so it should be [I].
   - The difficulty and integration results rest on 2–8 apps per subgroup (p. 6), yet are rated "moderate".
   - The frontmatter's "31.8–93.6% agreement" range includes a human–human figure.
   - The analysed PDF is arXiv v3, not the ACM version. Its abstract says the validation split is "private" while the metadata abstract says "public".
4. **zhao2025vibe:**
   - The claim that Gemini 2.5 Pro is most secure (30.4%) is measured only on tasks all four models solved. That subset is at most about 24–37 tasks per framework, is never reported, and is biased to easy tasks. The strength should drop to weak.
   - `metadata.json` still says preprint although the paper is ICML 2026. This needs a fix through `rlab`, not by hand.
5. **xiao2025benchmarking:**
   - The header lists 6 authors; the PDF and metadata list 9 (Zhiyao Xu, Yuhang Wang and Michael R. Lyu are missing).
   - The evidence row says the usability rates are "on 374 interactions", which contradicts its own §6 note that the number of evaluated items is not reported.
6. **Version drift:** tran, xiao, zhou and zhu cite a published DOI but were analysed from an arXiv copy. zhou2025declarui is analysed from arXiv v1 although the published ACM journal version is probably open access; its suspicious ablation table may have been corrected there. Standards §3 says to use the published version when one exists.

**Remaining fixes (smaller):**
- **mota2026comparing:** the outlier project changes the raw issue ranking but not the effort ranking. The "narrow base" critique is overstated. "More than half the effort comes from rule S1874" is an author claim, so [A].
- **wu2026looks:**
   - The 55 human-labelled scenarios were labelled by the authors themselves ("We labelled", p. 13).
   - Wrong page ref: p. 9 should be dropped from the annotation-figure refs.
   - "No self-preference observed" should be [A].
- **yang2026programbench:** "cheated" should be "flagged as cheating"; judges disagreed on 40–57% of tasks. The probing-share figure applies to 4 models, not all 9.
- **zhu2026understanding:**
   - "Across all stages and scenarios" should be [A].
   - The arXiv title differs from the metadata title, so the DOI-to-PDF link needs confirming.
   - The p-values support n ≈ 20.

**Cross-paper observations** (written into the report, all as [I] where interpretive):
- In four papers the model family that built the benchmark or judges the results also wins (yang, tran, wu, zhao). This is a shared RQ4 weakness.
- Iterative feedback looks contradictory across papers: in pan, one-shot repair strategies hurt quality, while in tran, zhou and wu, agentic or compiler loops help. Record both sides under "Contradictions".
- Design2Code and Interaction2Code both draw pages from the C4 validation set, so they may share source pages.
- zhu2026understanding disputes the SonarQube-based conclusions of Santa Molison et al. (project key molison2025llm); check that analysis during RQ3 synthesis.
- Contamination handling is uneven. Only Interaction2Code runs an explicit check, and it is weak. This is a possible gap, but it needs a novelty check before it can be claimed.

The report gives, per key, the section, current text, problem and corrected text with page refs. No `analysis.md` files were edited.
